First, this section formalizes the interaction between cryptographic mathematical constraints and the recursive nature of value-based learning; second, it introduces the Homomorphic Advantage Operator (HAO) to resolve these constraints, then proves its formal properties, and lastly outlines the client-server deployment architecture. Figure 1 provides a high-level overview of the proposed framework. Figure 1: High-level overview of the HAO framework for privacy-preserving reinforcement learning. The system integrates three interdependent components: (1) CKKS-encrypted state transmission and polynomial forward evaluation, (2) the HAO centering projection that neutralizes Bellman drift, and (3) clipped weight updates with optional DP-SGD-style Gaussian noise. We define the privacy-preserving RL agent as a deep Q-network mapping environmental states to a vector of action values. To ensure compatibility with the HE scheme, the network is restricted to a degree- d polynomial activation function P d P_{d} . For the mechanical constraint, we model the polynomial bottleneck at the primary hidden layer, where the forward pass is defined as: Q ⁡ ( s , ⋅ , θ ) = P d ​ ( s ​ W 1 + b 1 ) ​ W 2 + b 2 Q(s,\cdot;\theta)=P_{d}(sW_{1}+b_{1})W_{2}+b_{2} (3) where θ = { W 1 , b 1 , W 2 , b 2 } \theta=\{W_{1},b_{1},W_{2},b_{2}\} denotes the network parameters, s s is the environmental state, and the dot ( ⋅ \cdot ) indicates that Q ⁡ ( s , ⋅ , θ ) ∈ ℝ | 𝒜 | Q(s,\cdot;\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{A}|} represents the vector of Q-values evaluated across all possible actions in the action space 𝒜 \mathcal{A} with cardinality | 𝒜 | |\mathcal{A}| . Additionally, P d P_{d} is a degree- d d Chebyshev approximation of the ReLU function. This approximation is mathematically valid only within a strictly bounded domain [ − B , B ] [-B,B] . Consequently, the pre-activation vector z 1 = s ​ W 1 + b 1 z_{1}=sW_{1}+b_{1} must satisfy the hard constraint ‖ z 1 ‖ ∞ ≤ B \|z_{1}\|_{\infty}\leq B , ∥ ⋅ ∥ ∞ \|\cdot\|_{\infty} is the supremum norm, to prevent the polynomial divergence. Theorem 1 (Bellman Drift Bound) . For a γ \gamma -discounted MDP with a per-step polynomial approximation error bounded by ϵ a ​ p ​ p \epsilon_{app} , the steady-state value function error satisfies: ‖ Q ∗ − Q ^ ‖ ∞ ≤ ϵ a ​ p ​ p 1 − γ \|Q^{*}-\hat{Q}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\epsilon_{app}}{1-\gamma} (4) where Q ∗ Q^{*} represents the optimal action-value function, Q ^ \hat{Q} denotes the approximated value function under the polynomial evaluation, and ∥ ⋅ ∥ ∞ \|\cdot\|_{\infty} is the supremum norm. This theoretical upper bound adapts the finite-time analysis of approximate value iteration established by Munos and Szepesvári [ 22 ] , proving that even marginal polynomial deviations are severely amplified by the recursive nature of the Bellman operator. To understand why traditional neural network regularization fails to prevent this amplification, we must examine the internal structure of the action values. Any Q-value can be structurally decomposed as Q ⁡ ( s , a ) = V ⁡ ( s ) + A ⁡ ( s , a ) Q(s,a)=V(s)+A(s,a) , where V ⁡ ( s ) = 1 | 𝒜 | ​ ∑ a ′ Q ⁡ ( s , a ′ ) V(s)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{a^{\prime}}Q(s,a^{\prime}) is the state-value baseline and A ⁡ ( s , a ) = Q ⁡ ( s , a ) − V ⁡ ( s ) A(s,a)=Q(s,a)-V(s) represents the relative advantage of an action [ 32 ] . In practical environments, the magnitude of the state-value baseline typically dwarfs the advantage function, meaning | V ⁡ ( s ) | ≫ | A ⁡ ( s , a ) | |V(s)|\gg|A(s,a)| . Standard stabilization techniques such as L2 weight decay and gradient clipping successfully control overall weight magnitude but fail to eliminate the persistent directional pressure exerted by V ⁡ ( s ) V(s) . Every TD update systematically pulls the network weights toward this large uniform baseline. This asymmetric force inevitably overpowers symmetric weight decay. The vulnerability is particularly pronounced in environments with dense continuous state spaces, such as logistics routing. Because all input features activate simultaneously, they rapidly accelerate pre-activation growth, virtually guaranteeing a catastrophic breach of the boundary B B . 3.1 The Homomorphic Advantage Operator (HAO) To overcome the theoretical limitations of standard regularization, we introduce the Homomorphic Advantage Operator (HAO). This operator structurally eliminates the persistent Bellman drift without introducing prohibitive computational overhead to the HE circuit. The method integrates a zero-depth centering projection with symmetric regularization. items.raw_text: Homomorphic Advantage Operator: Stabilizing Reinforcement Learning Under Fully Homomorphic Encryption Constraints Abid Mohamed Nadhir abid-mohamednadhir@univ-eloued.dz Ahmad Al Hanbali ahmad.alhanbali@kfupm.edu.sa Beggas Mounir beggas-mounir@univ-eloued.dz organization=El Oued University, city=El Oued, country=Algeria organization=King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals (KFUPM), city=Dhahran, country=Saudi Arabia organization=Interdisciplinary Research Center For Smart Mobility and Logistics, KFUPM, city=Dhahran, country=Saudi Arabia Abstract Privacy-preserving machine learning presents significant deployment challenges on the cloud for intelligent systems with confidential data. Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) offers a compelling solution for secure computation, preserving data confidentiality of cloud computations. However, applying FHE to reinforcement learning (RL) requires replacing non-linear operations with polynomial approximations, which diverge catastrophically due to a unique recursive error phenomenon known as the Bellman drift. This article introduces the Homomorphic Advantage Operator (HAO), a stabilization framework designed to prevent polynomial approximation divergence in FHE-based deep RL. HAO adapts the zero-mean centering projection from advantage-based value estimation directly to temporal-difference (TD) targets. This linear projection annihilates the uniform state-value baseline that drives the Bellman drift, maintaining per-state action rankings while requiring zero additional non-linear multiplicative depth and avoiding expensive ciphertext bootstrapping. The proposed HAO framework was evaluated using a three-tier experimental methodology, including a tabular Markov Decision Process (MDP), an encrypted CartPole environment using real CKKS cryptographic operations, and a 20-node logistics routing benchmark with dense continuous features. The results demonstrate that the proposed HAO strictly bounds network pre-activations within the safe polynomial approximation domain. The proposed HAO RL agents achieved 0% boundary breaches across all random seeds used, whereas regularization alone (L2 weight decay and gradient clipping) breached the bound on 3 of 5 seeds and the unstabilized baseline did so in 83.8% of episodes. Finally, HAO agents improve optimal policy accuracy by 18.0 percentage points in tabular domains and remain stable when DP-SGD-style Gaussian noise is added to the clipped gradients. keywords Homomorphic encryption ,Reinforcement learning ,Polynomial activation ,Privacy-preserving machine learning ,Bellman operator ,Advantage function † † corresponding: Corresponding author 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful tool for optimizing complex, dynamic systems, from autonomous robotics to large-scale industrial supply chains and logistics [ 31 , 7 , 28 ] . However, as these intelligent systems are increasingly deployed in cloud environments, they face stringent data privacy and confidentiality requirements. In scenarios such as smart logistics routing, transmitting sensitive operational data, like proprietary demand forecasts, financial data, or real-time vehicle GPS coordinates, to centralized servers presents critical security vulnerabilities [ 18 , 17 ] . Recent work has shown that CKKS-based encryption can protect such location data in outsourced services such as ride-sharing and traffic management [ 33 ] . Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) offers a compelling solution to this privacy bottleneck by enabling computation directly on encrypted data [ 8 ] . Under an FHE paradigm, a client can encrypt their operational state and transmit ciphertexts to a cloud-hosted neural network, which then computes and returns encrypted policy decisions without ever exposing the underlying raw data [ 9 , 15 ] . While we refer to this broad paradigm as FHE, our practical implementation utilizes Leveled Homomorphic Encryption (LHE). By exploiting the fixed depth of the neural network architecture, LHE avoids the prohibitive computational cost of ciphertext bootstrapping, enabling efficient real-time policy evaluation. Despite its cryptographic guarantees, a fundamental limitation of FHE schemes such as CKKS is that they natively support only addition and multiplication [ 8 ] . Consequently, standard non-linear activation functions like ReLU or sigmoid must be replaced with polynomial approximations [ 27 , 3 ] . The standard approach utilizes degree- d d Chebyshev polynomials, which provide minimax approximation over a strictly bounded convergence domain [ − B , B ] [-B,B] [ 9 , 3 ] . For a degree-2 polynomial evaluated on [ − 5 , 5 ] [-5,5] : P 2 ​ ( z ) = 0.469 + 0.5 ​ z + 0.094 ​ z 2 ≈ max ⁡ ( 0 , z ) P_{2}(z)=0.469+0.5z+0.094z^{2}\approx\max(0,z) (1) If the neural network’s pre-activation functions move out-of-bounds [ − B , B ] [-B,B] , the higher-order polynomial terms cause catastrophic numerical explosion [ 3 , 16 ] . For example, at z = 50 z=50 , P 2 ​ ( 50 ) = 260.47 P_{2}(50)=260.47 compared to ReLU ​ ( 50 ) = 50 \text{ReLU}(50)=50 . This failure mode is well-documented in FHE-based supervised learning, where solutions include boundary loss penalties [ 3 ] , trainable polynomial coefficients [ 27 ] , and modified training methodologies [ 4 ] . None of the supervised-learning solutions addresses the unique dynamics of RL, and existing privacy-preserving RL frameworks [ 24 , 25 ] do not target the polynomial activation divergence caused by recursive temporal-difference (TD) bootstrapping. In supervised learning, target labels are fixed, static constants. In RL, the TD targets are computed sequentially from the network’s own outputs via bootstrapping [ 31 ] : y t = r t + γ ​ max a ⁡ Q ⁡ ( s t + 1 , a , θ ) y_{t}=r_{t}+\gamma\max_{a}Q(s_{t+1},a;\theta) (2) where r t r_{t} is the transition reward, γ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ) \gamma\in[0,1) is the discount factor, and Q ⁡ ( s t + 1 , a ′ , θ ) Q(s_{t+1},a^{\prime};\theta) evaluates next-state actions under current network parameters θ \theta . Because each forward pass through the encrypted network injects a small polynomial approximation error, ϵ a ​ p ​ p \epsilon_{app} . Because the target depends on the Q Q values computed with the polynomial, the error accumulates recursively throughout training. The resulting steady-state value function error is bounded by ‖ Q ∗ − Q ^ ‖ ∞ ≤ ϵ a ​ p ​ p / ( 1 − γ ) \|Q^{*}-\hat{Q}\|_{\infty}\leq\epsilon_{app}/(1-\gamma) [ 5 , 22 ] . At a standard discount factor of γ = 0.99 \gamma=0.99 , this results in a 100 × 100\times amplification of the polynomial error. The error amplification creates a positive feedback loop—which we formally term the Bellman drift—that pushes pre-activation values out of the Chebyshev boundary, rendering standard FHE architectures numerically unstable. To address this instability, the zero-mean advantage centering principle was applied directly to the temporal-difference bootstrapping targets while employing dueling architectures [ 32 ] . Note that the dueling architectures perform internal stream centering for network identifiability; however, they still output drift-prone Q Q -values. Our approach tackles this shortcoming by introducing a holistic architectural framework for privacy-preserving RL. Our specific contributions are as follows: 1. We identify and formally define the Bellman drift as an RL-specific failure mode under FHE polynomial constraints, distinguishing it from the static approximation errors found in supervised learning literature. 2. We propose the Homomorphic Advantage Operator (HAO), a tripartite stabilization framework. It adapts the zero-mean advantage centering principle of Dueling architectures [ 32 ] , but shifts its application directly to the value recursion. Whereas dueling networks perform internal stream centering for network identifiability while still outputting full drift-prone Q Q -values, HAO applies a zero-mean linear projection matrix P P directly to the temporal-difference bootstrapping targets. This projection purges the uniform state-value baseline V ⁡ ( s ) V(s) from the recursive error loop, thus eliminating Bellman drift with no additional multiplicative depth. When paired with client-side reward scaling and decoupled weight decay, HAO strictly bounds pre-activations within degree-2 polynomial limits without requiring ciphertext bootstrapping. 3. We demonstrate through a three-tier experimental evaluation, including a tabular MDP, a CartPole environment using real TenSEAL CKKS cryptographic operations, and a single-depot capacitated routing benchmark, that the HAO framework achieves 0% boundary breaches, whereas regularization alone breaches the bound on 3 of 5 random seeds and the unstabilized baseline in 83.8% of episodes. 4. We show that the HAO framework remains stable when Gaussian noise of the kind used in DP-SGD is added to the clipped gradients ( σ \sigma up to 1.0), which makes it compatible with differentially private training. The remaining part of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 , the related literature is reviewed. Section 3 explains the proposed methodology in detail. Section 4 evaluates the proposed framework numerically. In section 5 , we discuss the main findings and key insights. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper, including possible future extensions. 2 Related Work This section reviews the existing literature surrounding secure machine learning and cryptographic protocols. We categorize prior contributions into three distinct areas: techniques for managing polynomial activations under HE constraints, foundational cryptographic methodologies, and prior efforts in privacy-preserving RL. As summarized in Table 1 , while extensive research addresses stability in supervised learning and static inference, the unique challenges of applying FHE to RL remain unexplored. CryptoNets [ 9 ] introduced the use of square activations ( x 2 x^{2} ) for HE-compatible inference. Subsequent work improved accuracy through self-learning activation functions (SLAF) [ 27 , 34 ] , HE-friendly training with knowledge distillation [ 4 ] , and boundary loss penalties with selective gradient clipping [ 3 ] . The ReBoot framework [ 26 ] enables fully encrypted training via depth-minimized architectures with CKKS bootstrapping. Crucially, the previous stabilization methods are explicitly designed for supervised learning paradigms. Boundary loss penalties and SLAF rely on the assumption that target labels are static, ground-truth constants provided by a dataset. In RL, the agent generates its own dynamic targets via temporal-difference (TD) bootstrapping. The static training-time regularizers are insufficient to prevent the subsequent Bellman drift because the targets themselves are impacted by the polynomial approximation error. The CKKS scheme [ 8 ] supports approximate arithmetic on encrypted real numbers, serving as the foundation for our continuous state-space operations. Alternate approaches include GAZELLE [ 15 ] , which combines HE linear layers with garbled circuits for exact non-linear operations, and Glyph [ 20 ] , which switches between CKKS and TFHE schemes to optimize different operation types. While mathematically robust, these mixed-protocol techniques incur significant communication and computational overhead, rendering them difficult to scale for highly sequential RL environments. Prior work on privacy-preserving RL can be categorized into three distinct paradigms as follows: (I) Several cryptographic data-protection approaches utilizing Multi-Party Computation (MPC) or Differential Privacy (DP) are proposed to protect distributed parameters. Namely, federated RL frequently deploys secure aggregation to mask client weight updates [ 6 ] , while DP-SGD bounds gradient privacy leakage [ 1 ] . Homomorphic encryption has likewise been used to protect gradients in distributed and federated deep learning [ 2 , 10 ] . However, these approaches do not provide a mechanism for an untrusted cloud server to compute policy forward passes directly on encrypted continuous state features. (II) A growing body of work explores direct evaluation on encrypted data. For example, Park et al. [ 25 ] proposed a privacy-preserving Q-learning framework using LWE-based FHE in cloud computing, validating feasibility on tabular problems but without neural-network function approximation or polynomial activations. Liu et al. [ 19 ] introduced the Preyer framework for dynamic treatment regimes, designing a plaintext length control protocol to manage bit-length overflow during repeated encrypted operations in small discrete state spaces. Jesu et al. [ 14 ] studied DQN training over AES-encrypted state inputs; notably, they evaluated homomorphic encryption (CKKS) but concluded that its computational latency was infeasible for iterative RL, falling back to symmetric block ciphers where performance collapsed on complex environments. Most recently, Nguyen et al. [ 24 ] introduced a groundbreaking privacy-preserving Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) framework using CKKS with full bootstrapping, achieving performance within 10% of plaintext baselines on CartPole and Pendulum cases. Their core innovation is an HE-compatible Adam optimizer that reparameterizes momentum to bypass high-degree polynomial approximations of inverse square roots. However, their framework requires high-degree minimax polynomials (degrees 15 and 31) and full bootstrapping (incurring ≈ 505 \approx 505 s per training step on CartPole), and does not analyze whether pre-activations remain within the polynomial approximation domain. (III) RL is increasingly applied to security problems themselves [ 13 ] , and recent studies investigate RL for FHE compilation rather than RL under FHE constraints. Sefsaf et al. [ 29 ] utilize deep RL as a compiler optimization tool to automate FHE code vectorization, where the RL agent operates in plaintext. Similarly, Sun et al. [ 30 ] deploy FHE strictly for secure gradient aggregation in usage-based insurance, while policy evaluations remain in plaintext. Table 1 summarizes the surveyed solutions across supervised learning, cryptographic schemes, and privacy-preserving RL. While prior RL works address optimization bottlenecks [ 24 ] or tabular feasibility [ 25 ] , none of them addresses the recursive polynomial activation explosion (Bellman drift) inherent to bootstrapped deep Q-learning. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to formalize this activation-domain failure mode and provide a zero-depth linear operator that enables stable deep RL under lightweight computations of degree-2 leveled HE, while avoiding costly bootstrapping evaluations. items.content: Research Our research teams investigate the safety, inner workings, and societal impacts of AI models—so that artificial intelligence has a positive impact as it becomes increasingly capable. Research teams: Alignment Economics Interpretability Societal Impacts Frontier Red Team Alignment The Alignment team works to understand the risks of AI models and develop ways to ensure that future ones remain helpful, honest, and harmless. Economics The Economics team studies how AI is reshaping the economy, including work, productivity, and economic opportunity. Frontier Red Team The Frontier Red Team analyzes the implications of frontier AI models for cybersecurity, biosecurity, and autonomous systems. Interpretability The mission of the Interpretability team is to understand how large language models work internally, as a foundation for AI safety and positive outcomes. Societal Impacts Working closely with the Anthropic Policy and Safeguards teams, Societal Impacts is a technical research team that explores how AI is used in the real world. Scenarios for our Economic Future Anthropic’s Economics team is sharing a new model of how AI may affect economic growth, jobs, wages, and more by 2030. The model lets you explore the scenarios, tell us what you think will happen, and see how your answers compare to +10,000 Americans. Science Sep 23, 2026 Claude discovers a novel enzyme system with CRISPR-like repeats We’re announcing a new life sciences research group and laboratory at Anthropic. This post introduces the team behind this work and shares early results in which Claude discovered a novel enzyme system with properties reminiscent of CRISPR, with only high-level direction from our scientists. Sep 17, 2026 Measurements for understanding the pace of AI development inside frontier labs Today, the world can’t see what’s going on inside AI labs. Anthropic is proposing new metrics that would give the public visibility into frontier AI development. Science Sep 4, 2026 Formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem We are sharing the first complete computer-checked proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem. Claude worked largely autonomously over 11 days to write the proof in the Lean programming language. Alignment Sep 9, 2026 An alignment assessment of recent cybersecurity incidents We present an alignment assessment of four incidents in which Claude models gained unauthorized access to real third-party systems. items.content: Science Claude-shaped science Oct 1, 2026 Summary: In this guest post, Prof. Matthew Schwartz returns to describe a new approach to AI-accelerated science. In Vibe Physics , Schwartz discussed similarities in capability between Claude and a physics graduate student. Here, he describes what happened when he stopped fighting Claude and allowed Claude to find “Claude-shaped” problems: ones best suited to the capabilities of the current generation of LLM tools. This led him to build BootLoops, a toolkit for exact calculations in quantitative science. Because similar calculations often turn up across very disparate areas of science, Claude found connections to ecology, population genetics, and a dozen other fields. These connections were often technically correct but scientifically unremarkable at first, so Schwartz worked with domain experts to steer BootLoops toward questions those fields care about. Below, we share more about these projects and how BootLoops came about. Agentic AI is improving rapidly. Everyone notices the models seem smarter: they know more, make fewer mistakes, and have better ideas. If you follow the trend lines, it is easy to speak confidently about the potential of AI to revolutionize science. However, academic scientists trying to use the models today in their own work often feel a disconnect. The models may be solving challenging and longstanding problems , but so far these have mostly been well-scoped applications of existing techniques. Many of the headlines seem to be in mathematics, the one part of science where a problem can be stated completely and an answer checked absolutely. But most of science is not like that. And for many of us researchers and students, the distance between those headlines and what happens when we use these models can leave us frustrated and anxious. The core conflict, as I see it, is that although these models are brilliant, working like a human scientist is not what current LLMs do best. Claude and GPT are good at science, but they are not scientists : yes, they are smart, but it can take a lot of hand-holding to get them to produce anything of scientific value. Physicists would call this an “impedance mismatch”: two systems that each work fine but are poorly matched, so most of what one puts in never gets through to the other. Here, the mismatch is between what scientists want and what AI does well. So how can we fix it? I started looking for examples where the impedance mismatches are less acute. I began by having Claude build an accessible suite of tools for mathematical physics. Before long, the tools found uses for other problems. This iterative process generated a set of software and scientific protocols, which I call BootLoops. BootLoops functions as a kind of harness for the LLM, much like Claude Code or Claude Science is a harness for Claude, or Codex is a harness for GPT. I’ve found BootLoops especially well-suited for a class of quantitative problems in science. It is also open-source, so it can be used with whatever model you like. The current generation of AI tools is not capable of solving most problems in science. However, they are astonishingly good at certain “agentic-AI-shaped” problems. Once Claude had BootLoops, it kept noticing the same pattern: many fields have problems that a technique from mathematics, physics, or computer science would solve outright if anyone knew it existed. I started calling these “Claude-shaped” problems, and followed them outside high-energy theoretical physics—my home turf—into geology, biology, economics, and linguistics. In these other areas, I could not rely on my own expertise to know whether what Claude found was interesting. So I found some experts and asked. With their guidance, BootLoops was able to make substantive advances in many research areas. Below, I share how BootLoops came about, describe some early findings in areas where I have been applying it, and share some of my thinking on how to resolve the impedance mismatch between human and AI scientists today. Claude, take the wheel! Last December, I tried using Claude as a research assistant , and found that Claude Opus 4.5 performed like a strong graduate student at 20 times the speed. Despite Claude producing a high-quality paper at the end of the experiment, it was a slog to get there. I had to correct every sentence it wrote, steer it away from irrelevant threads, and pull it back from dead ends. This summer, I tried doing something different: instead of treating Claude like the collaborator I wanted it to be, I started to treat it like the collaborator it actually is. This required looking for problems suited to its strengths. Right now, Claude is just not able to help me with deep conceptual questions—but it does have a virtually unlimited breadth of knowledge across all domains, incredible coding skills, leading-edge knowledge of mathematics and statistics, and the ability to parse papers, appendices, and data at machine speed. A natural place to start looking for Claude-shaped problems was in areas where coding could help. When Anthropic released Claude Fable 5 in Summer 2026, I wanted to see whether its cyber capabilities would translate to scientific computing. So I sought to test it by having it port, code up, and improve various methods from a handful of my papers and the adjacent literature on scattering amplitudes. Scattering amplitudes are how we interpret data from the Large Hadron Collider: smash two protons at 13 trillion electron volts, and the amplitude is the theoretical bridge between the debris and whatever new particle, a Higgs boson or something unknown, the collision produced. At their core are Feynman diagrams, multidimensional integrals of a particular form. The ones we are struggling with now can each be a PhD thesis, or occupy a group for years. Over the past 20 years an alternative has grown up: the S-matrix bootstrap. In the bootstrap approach, instead of grinding out the integral, you impose physical constraints until only one answer is possible. Knowing where the amplitude is infinite (its “singularities”) might narrow it to 20,000 options; a symmetry cuts that to 500; and so on down to one. The traditional bootstrap is purely analytic and has gone furthest in the most symmetric theories, where the constraints reach all the way to a single option (the nine-loop amplitude in N=4 super-Yang–Mills is an example). Closer to the real world you often run out of constraints before the end. A newer pivot , the semi-numerical bootstrap, closes the gap when you can also compute the amplitude at a handful of points to absurd precision (sometimes 1,000 digits): if few enough options remain, those numbers pin down the remaining coefficients exactly. The semi-numerical bootstrap seemed ideal for agentic AI. It draws on mathematics, physics, and computer science that no one person has mastered; it needs a great deal of coding and algorithm development; and it is checkable, since the same numerics let anyone, expert or not, verify the final answer against the integral to as many digits as they like by running two scripts. The community's expertise is also unevenly distributed: good ideas sit in Wolfram Language, C++, Python, or Julia, and many more sit in papers with no code at all. So my first assignment for Fable 5 was to port all of it to a common framework, and to write the code the papers never provided. Claude did this effortlessly. I was surprised when it reproduced the results from my paper in around 20 minutes, while the code I wrote to do it took me weeks. However, I was not surprised when it informed me that I was doing something very inefficiently and that there was a better algorithm I was unaware of. Then, I asked Claude to search for unsolved amplitudes it could compute. It turns out that problems that are simple enough for the S-matrix bootstrap are also simple enough for humans to do—and, indeed, most have been done. It nevertheless found a few unsolved problems. After some discussion with the model, it became clear that Claude was limiting itself to amplitudes with the simplest family of functions: logarithms. So I asked, could it do the same thing for the next simplest family, elliptic functions? Elliptic integrals are really hard, even for people like me who spend a lot of their time computing integrals. Only a handful of elliptic Feynman integrals have ever been computed, and none completely by the bootstrap, at least to my or Claude’s knowledge. The issue is not that the methods wouldn’t work, but rather that nobody had tried, since the expertise needed to do so is distributed among many humans. Claude, by contrast, easily generalized all of the machinery it had ported and built for the logarithmic case to these other integral classes. This time it wrote most of the software itself, or borrowed it from mathematics rather than physics. As the toolkit grew, it started to land one integral after another. Soon we had 30 integrals BootLooped from end to end, comprising 15 reproductions of known results by this new method and 15 that had never before been computed. That was all after only a few weeks. Initially, I thought I would be satisfied just to do a write-up on that, but I was too tempted to see what else we (that is, me and Claude with BootLoops) could do. “I know Kung Fu” A serendipitous feature of science is that the same equations often appear over and over again in different contexts. In physics, for example, the diffusion equation, Fokker-Planck equation, and Schrödinger equation all have the same mathematical form, so if you develop a method to solve one problem, you can often apply it to many others. I knew that computations BootLoops was good at were relevant elsewhere: in cosmology and string theory, for example. What I didn’t know, but Claude was happy to tell me, was that these integrals could also map onto Bayesian evidence integrals in population genetics, or that the finite-field methods used for Feynman integral reduction could also apply to problems in evolutionary biology. This kicked off a particularly fertile period of searching for and solving Claude-shaped (and, more narrowly, BootLoops-shaped) problems. Some ideas were immediately obvious as great applications. For example, the science of phylogenetics studies how to organize species into family trees using DNA; the relevant computation is a Bayesian evidence integral, whose output is a single number saying how well a candidate tree accounts for the observed DNA, an integral of the same kind BootLoops was originally built to do. As the ideas came, I insisted that Claude both use old tools and build new ones, so that the harness would grow. Each tool, even from a failed project, opened up new doors. Claude was getting more and more capable. It was like Neo in The Matrix after waking up from the Kung Fu download. As the projects drifted from my professional comfort zone, however, I started to worry. Another project involved looking at exact calculations in population genetics, a field that studies how genes vary within a population and why. Claude first used methods imported from mathematical physics to solve a 30-year-old integral expression for how natural selection shapes rare mutations. We applied it to gnomAD , the largest public catalog of human genetic variation. Claude was very excited about this result, but I wasn’t so sure. Other projects had a similar arc: Claude comes up with an initial finding I find compelling. I bring it to an expert, who is unmoved but sees the potential, and together we sculpt it into meaningful science. Interestingly, some of these drifted from BootLoops-shaped quantitative calculations to more general Claude-shaped work. For example: Economics . Some additional highlights, each of which was done in collaboration with experts, and each of which is undergoing further exploration and verification, include: Phylogenetics. We made the Bayesian evidence for evolutionary trees fast to compute and exactly checkable, and found that single genes are often tied between competing trees by less than the error of standard sampling programs. Earth science . We combined equations and data from atmospheric science, geochemistry, and climate modeling to build a quantitative, predictive model of how the Great Oxidation Event unfolded through four glaciations. The technical details Running many projects at once (36 manuscripts in 18 fields with 19 coauthors over three months, out of some 400 candidate problems) takes a lot of coordination, both for me and for Claude. The setup that makes this manageable is fairly simple. The Claude Code sessions all run in terminals on Google Cloud virtual machines, linked to various GitHub and Overleaf repos depending on my collaborators’ preferences. I have separate sessions for each project, plus a master session that coordinates the others, allocates compute, and validates results. Each session involves agents that run the computations in the background, with intermediate results stored in markdown files in their respective folders. These subagents are helpful because I regularly run into Fable 5’s classifiers; instead of these blocks corrupting my whole session, they just shut down a single agent. I also have separate sessions for writing results; creating the GitHub repos, tool manuals, and the BootLoops website; writing and validating all the separate tool codes; and checking and rechecking results as an adversarial referee. A bigger problem was that Claude’s default approach seemed to be to try to grind through a long, multiday calculation rather than build a new tool that would make that same calculation take mere minutes. Time and again, I had to tell it to think smarter, not harder. Over the course of these long projects, compaction would often kick in, causing Claude to lose important context. To guard against this, I had Claude periodically organize its files and consolidate them, so it always had access to the latest version of the plan. On one project, it was proud of its proof, up to “one unproven lemma.” That lemma was the whole proof! I said no unproven lemmas. Then “done” again, but now with a new axiom. Have it explain what it found until you believe it. Supply the taste. Claude can find Claude-shaped problems, but there are thousands, perhaps millions, of them. Claude seems to favor old debates, highly cited but long forgotten. Asking it to focus on what is newly possible , not what is merely faster or involves more digits, helps, but you still can’t trust its judgment of whether something is interesting. Follow up. Once Claude has a great result, ask for an even greater one. It will always come up with something, and occasionally it’s brilliant. Watch out for the grind. Instead, I developed a sense of how long something interesting should take, and I learned to sense whether Claude was making what I considered progress on a sensible time scale. I hope the BootLoops harness can be used broadly across quantitative science without each user having to rebuild everything from scratch. Agentic AI makes it easier to connect ideas and share codebases, and if we learn to use that strength, the community can move faster than any individual could alone. Everyone notices the models seem smarter: they know more, make fewer mistakes, and have better ideas. If you follow the trend lines, it is easy to speak confidently about the potential of AI to revolutionize science. However, academic scientists trying to use the models today in their own work often feel a disconnect. The models may be solving challenging and longstanding problems , but so far these have mostly been well-scoped applications of existing techniques. Many of the headlines seem to be in mathematics, the one part of science where a problem can be stated completely and an answer checked absolutely. But most of science is not like that. And for many of us researchers and students, the distance between those headlines and what happens when we use these models can leave us frustrated and anxious. The core conflict, as I see it, is that although these models are brilliant, working like a human scientist is not what current LLMs do best. Claude and GPT are good at science, but they are not scientists : yes, they are smart, but it can take a lot of hand-holding to get them to produce anything of scientific value. Physicists would call this an “impedance mismatch”: two systems that each work fine but are poorly matched, so most of what one puts in never gets through to the other. Here, the mismatch is between what scientists want and what AI does well. So how can we fix it? I started looking for examples where the impedance mismatches are less acute. I began by having Claude build an accessible suite of tools for mathematical physics. Before long, the tools found uses for other problems. This iterative process generated a set of software and scientific protocols, which I call BootLoops. BootLoops functions as a kind of harness for the LLM, much like Claude Code or Claude Science is a harness for Claude, or Codex is a harness for GPT. I’ve found BootLoops especially well-suited for a class of quantitative problems in science. It is also open-source, so it can be used with whatever model you like. The current generation of AI tools is not capable of solving most problems in science. However, they are astonishingly good at certain “agentic-AI-shaped” problems. Once Claude had BootLoops, it kept noticing the same pattern: many fields have problems that a technique from mathematics, physics, or computer science would solve outright if anyone knew it existed. I started calling these “Claude-shaped” problems, and followed them outside high-energy theoretical physics—my home turf—into geology, biology, economics, and linguistics. In these other areas, I could not rely on my own expertise to know whether what Claude found was interesting. So I found some experts and asked. With their guidance, BootLoops was able to make substantive advances in many research areas. Claude, take the wheel! Last December, I tried using Claude as a research assistant , and found that Claude Opus 4.5 performed like a strong graduate student at 20 times the speed. This required looking for problems suited to its strengths. Right now, Claude is just not able to help me with deep conceptual questions—but it does have a virtually unlimited breadth of knowledge across all domains, incredible coding skills, leading-edge knowledge of mathematics and statistics, and the ability to parse papers, appendices, and data at machine speed. A natural place to start looking for Claude-shaped problems was in areas where coding could help. When Anthropic released Claude Fable 5 in Summer 2026, I wanted to see whether its cyber capabilities would translate to scientific computing. So I sought to test it by having it port, code up, and improve various methods from a handful of my papers and the adjacent literature on scattering amplitudes. Scattering amplitudes are how we interpret data from the Large Hadron Collider: smash two protons at 13 trillion electron volts, and the amplitude is the theoretical bridge between the debris and whatever new particle, a Higgs boson or something unknown, the collision produced. Over the past 20 years an alternative has grown up: the S-matrix bootstrap. In the bootstrap approach, instead of grinding out the integral, you impose physical constraints until only one answer is possible.
