TACO: Ternary Absolute-max Column-wise One-sparse Optimizer for LLM Fine-Tuning Jichao Jiang Affiliation: University of Central Florida Cristian McGee Affiliation: University of Central Florida El Houcine Bergou Affiliation: Mohammed VI Polytechnic University Hanqin Cai & Aritra Dutta Affiliation: University of Central Florida Abstract Full-parameter fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) incurs substantial optimizer state memory overhead, limiting the model sizes that fit on modern GPUs. Existing approaches either compress optimizer state, abandon first-order gradients, or change the update geometry while retaining dense state. The recently introduced Muon optimizer reduces optimizer memory through matrix-valued updates. Still, its geometry differs from AdamW and can lead to performance degradation when fine-tuning AdamW-pretrained models. To reduce optimizer memory without sacrificing accuracy or computational efficiency in LLM fine-tuning, we propose T ernary A bsolute-max C olumn-wise O ne-sparse optimizer, or TACO , which follows Muon’s operator-norm steepest-descent view but takes the geometric route further. TACO computes the exact steepest-descent direction under a dimension-normalized → 1 1\!	o\!1 operator norm by selecting the sign of the largest magnitude entry in each column of two-dimensional weight matrices. This retains first-order gradients while making optimizer state memory nearly negligible. Our practical TACO optimizer maintains only a small set of low precision gradient components per column, reducing persistent optimizer state by 174 × 174	imes relative to AdamW8bit (from 27.7 27.7 GB to 0.16 0.16 GB) and peak training memory by 2.9 × 2.9	imes (from 80.6 80.6 GB to 27.5 27.5 GB) on OPT-13B, while achieving comparable accuracy and runtime. TACO further enables full-parameter fine-tuning of 30-32B-parameter models on a single 80 GB H100 GPU across multiple model families and tasks. Our code is available at: github.com/Jichao2357/TACO_optimizer . 1 Introduction Full-parameter fine-tuning adapts all model weights and remains a strong baseline for transferring large language models (LLMs) to downstream tasks ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ; Hu et al., 2021 ) ; however, it often suffers from memory overhead. For instance, a 13B-parameter model occupies roughly 26 GB of memory in BF16 before allocating any training state. During AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) fine-tuning, the two FP32 moment buffers add another ∼ \sim 104 GB of memory. At the same time, gradients contribute ∼ \sim 26 GB, yielding roughly 156 GB before accounting for activations, temporary workspaces, or an optional FP32 master copy; see the Pareto frontier memory-accuracy trade-off graph in Figure 1 . Thus, at this scale, AdamW’s persistent optimizer states alone require roughly 4 × 4	imes the BF16 parameter memory. Several memory-efficient first-order optimizers reduce this overhead while retaining backpropagation, including state-quantizers (AdamW8bit quantizes optimizer states ( Dettmers et al., 2021 ) ; FlashAdamW combines 8-bit optimizer states with a compact master-weight representation ( Gonzalez Ortiz et al., 2026 ) ), factorized second moment methods (Adafactor uses factorized second-moment estimates ( Shazeer and Stern, 2018 ) ), and low-rank gradient methods (GaLore projects gradients and optimizer states into a low-rank subspace ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , and APOLLO-Mini uses a rank-1 subspace to estimate adaptive scaling factors ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) ). In contrast, zeroth-order (ZO) methods avoid backpropagation and approach inference-level memory by estimating updates from forward evaluations ( Bergou et al., 2020 ; Bibi et al., 2020 ; Gorbunov et al., 2020 ; Cai et al., 2021 ; Malladi et al., 2023 ; Boucherouite et al., 2024 ) . Recent variants incorporate low-rank subspaces or curvature information to improve query efficiency ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) , but still require additional forward queries. The recently introduced Muon optimizer ( Jordan, 2024 ; Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024 ; Shah et al., 2025 ) asks a different question: what steepest-descent direction under a matrix geometry makes the update useful? Muon treats two-dimensional weights as matrices, retains a single momentum matrix, and orthogonalizes it to approximate a steepest-descent step under spectral geometry . This reduces optimizer memory relative to AdamW, although Muon’s state remains dense. Additionally, switching an AdamW-pretrained model to Muon during fine-tuning can degrade performance, a phenomenon called optimizer mismatch that is attributed to the different update geometries and implicit biases of the two optimizers ( Qu et al., 2026 ) . Zeroth-Order Muon (ZO-Muon) ( Lang et al., 2026 ) improves query efficiency, but as a zeroth-order method, it requires additional forward evaluations. Sequential evaluation for ZO methods can keep memory close to inference, but the additional function evaluations can increase computational and communication overhead, especially in distributed training or with larger batches. Thus, existing approaches, including Muon, expose a fundamental trade-off between the memory footprint of first-order training and the optimization efficiency of standard gradients, prompting a natural question: Can full-parameter fine-tuning retain first-order information and competitive wall-clock efficiency while making persistent optimizer-state memory nearly negligible? Figure 1: Performance–memory overview of TACO and other optimizers. Left: Pareto frontier memory-accuracy trade-off for fine-tuning OPT-13B on the SST-2 dataset on an 80 GB H100 GPU. TACO lies at the low-memory end of the Pareto frontier, achieving 94.22% accuracy with 27.54 GB of peak training memory. The dashed line connects the Pareto-optimal methods. The vertical line marks the 80 GB H100 memory limit. Adam achieves 95.3% accuracy with 254.8 GB of peak memory. Right: Peak GPU memory decomposition of TACO on OPT-30B across 8 downstream tasks. The bars show model state, optimizer state, and other transient memory across all eight downstream tasks. TACO’s optimizer state occupies only 0.267 GB, less than 0.5% of peak memory on each task, while the transient memory accounts for the variation across tasks. To answer this, we propose TACO , a T ernary A bsolute-max C olumn-wise O ne-sparse optimizer. Using the same operator-norm steepest-descent viewpoint as Muon, TACO is not just another memory-efficient optimizer ; TACO’s conceptual centerpiece is an optimization geometry whose exact steepest-descent direction has extreme structural sparsity. Under a dimension-normalized → 1 1\!	o\!1 operator norm, the corresponding dual geometry makes the steepest-descent direction separable across columns, and each column selects the sign of its largest-magnitude gradient coordinate. Thus, an m × n m	imes n update contains at most n n nonzeros. Although the TACO steepest-descent direction is one-sparse per column, minibatch gradients can make the selected coordinates unstable across training. A conventional dense gradient history can stabilize coordinate selection but erodes the memory advantage. TACO instead retains only a small, low-precision set of dynamic gradient heavy hitters per column. This sparse gradient history keeps persistent optimizer-state memory negligible even as model size grows. For example, TACO can fine-tune OPT-30B on a single 80 GB H100 GPU, with peak GPU memory of 62.5 GB on SST-2, 64.7 GB on RTE, and 68.1 GB on BoolQ; see Peak GPU memory decomposition in Figure 1 . Adam does not fit this model on a single H100 80 GB GPU. Across our study, TACO enables full-parameter fine-tuning of models up to 32B parameters on a single 80 GB H100 and transfers across multiple model families and tasks. Taken together, our main contributions are: ( i ) Geometry-induced sparse optimization. We propose TACO, a new first-order optimizer for memory-efficient full-parameter LLM fine-tuning. TACO is derived from the exact steepest-descent solution under a dimension-normalized → 1 1\!	o\!1 operator norm, whose geometry naturally yields a ternary, column-wise Top-1 update. Thus, TACO’s sparsity is intrinsic to its optimization geometry rather than imposed by post-hoc gradient sparsification; see Section 3 . ( ii ) Convergence and fine-tuning theory. We prove that vanilla TACO reaches an ε \varepsilon -stationary point in 𝒪 ⁡ ( ε − 2 ) \mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}) iterations under standard smoothness assumptions. We further show that, in our theoretical setting, TACO shares the continuation geometry and limiting solution of an Adam proxy while differing from Muon, and satisfies standard μ \mu P spectral scaling under balanced winner counts. These results connect TACO to optimizer mismatch and the learning rate transfer problem; see Sections 3 and 4 . ( iii ) TACO-specific memory-efficient design. TACO does not require an accurate dense model of the gradient history, but only enough information to recover the dominant coordinate in each column. Exploiting this structure, we develop a practical implementation based on dynamic FP8 sparse gradient histories and immediate gradient processing, reducing persistent state from 𝒪 ⁡ ( m ​ n ) \mathcal{O}(mn) to 𝒪 ⁡ ( n ) \mathcal{O}(n) while retaining first-order gradients and the column-wise Top-1 update; see Section 5 . ( iv ) Empirical validation at scale. We evaluate TACO across model scales, architectures, and downstream tasks. TACO achieves competitive task performance with substantially reduced training memory, enables full-parameter fine-tuning of OPT-30B and Qwen3-32B on a single 80 GB H100 GPU, and transfers across OPT, Qwen3, Pythia, Llama, and Mistral model families. Ablations further characterize the roles of the gradient history EMA decay factor, heavy hitter threshold, update sparsity, and optimizer step budget; see Section 6 . 2 Related Work Zeroth-order optimization has become a practical way to reduce the memory cost of LLM fine-tuning. These methods construct an update direction from the change in loss under a parameter perturbation. MeZO applies this idea by regenerating its perturbations in place using a seeding trick ( Malladi et al., 2023 ) . Sparse MeZO reduces the number of perturbed parameters, preserving sparsity ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . ZO-Muon projects the estimated gradient into a lower-dimensional subspace and applies polar orthogonalization to recover more useful structure from the noisy estimate ( Lang et al., 2026 ) . HiZOO instead incorporates diagonal Hessian information into zeroth-order optimization, using curvature-aware preconditioning to improve convergence ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) . Memory-efficient first-order optimization methods retain backpropagation while reducing parameter-associated training state. Adafactor represents second moments using row and column factors ( Shazeer and Stern, 2018 ) , while CAME adds a confidence-guided correction to improve the stability of this representation ( Luo et al., 2023 ) . Alternatively, 8-bit Adam uses block-wise quantization to store optimizer statistics at lower precision ( Dettmers et al., 2021 ) . FlashOptim combines quantized optimizer states with a compact master-weight representation and provides FlashAdamW as a drop-in AdamW variant ( Gonzalez Ortiz et al., 2026 ) . GaLore projects gradients and optimizer states into a lower-dimensional space ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , whereas APOLLO approximates adaptive gradient scaling through a random low-rank auxiliary space; its APOLLO-Mini variant reduces this space to rank one and applies tensor-wise scaling ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) . Operator-norm and linear-minimization-oracle (LMO) optimization. Bernstein and Newhouse (2024) formulate matrix optimization as steepest-descent under operator norms and characterize the → p 1\!	o\!p family through maximum column norms. Pethick et al. (2025) develop a stochastic LMO framework and instantiate it with layer-aware operator geometries in Scion. Sign-based methods. In gradient compression, TernGrad maps gradient values to { − 1 , 0 , + 1 } \{-1,0,+1\} to reduce the communication bottleneck in distributed training ( Wen et al., 2017 ) , while signSGD retains only the coordinate-wise gradient signs ( Bernstein et al., 2018 ) ; see GRACE ( Xu et al., 2021 ) , a compressed communication framework that places these methods under one umbrella. SignMuon ( Mishra et al., 2026 ) communicates the signs of locally constructed Muon directions. 3 TACO: T ernary A bsolute-max C olumn-wise O ne-sparse Optimizer Setup and notation. TACO: Ternary Absolute-max Column-wise One-sparse Optimizer for LLM Fine-Tuning Jichao Jiang Affiliation: University of Central Florida Cristian McGee Affiliation: University of Central Florida El Houcine Bergou Affiliation: Mohammed VI Polytechnic University Hanqin Cai & Aritra Dutta Affiliation: University of Central Florida Abstract Full-parameter fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) incurs substantial optimizer state memory overhead, limiting the model sizes that fit on modern GPUs. Existing approaches either compress optimizer state, abandon first-order gradients, or change the update geometry while retaining dense state. The recently introduced Muon optimizer reduces optimizer memory through matrix-valued updates. Still, its geometry differs from AdamW and can lead to performance degradation when fine-tuning AdamW-pretrained models. To reduce optimizer memory without sacrificing accuracy or computational efficiency in LLM fine-tuning, we propose T ernary A bsolute-max C olumn-wise O ne-sparse optimizer, or TACO , which follows Muon’s operator-norm steepest-descent view but takes the geometric route further. TACO computes the exact steepest-descent direction under a dimension-normalized → 1 1\!	o\!1 operator norm by selecting the sign of the largest magnitude entry in each column of two-dimensional weight matrices. This retains first-order gradients while making optimizer state memory nearly negligible. Our practical TACO optimizer maintains only a small set of low precision gradient components per column, reducing persistent optimizer state by 174 × 174	imes relative to AdamW8bit (from 27.7 27.7 GB to 0.16 0.16 GB) and peak training memory by 2.9 × 2.9	imes (from 80.6 80.6 GB to 27.5 27.5 GB) on OPT-13B, while achieving comparable accuracy and runtime. TACO further enables full-parameter fine-tuning of 30-32B-parameter models on a single 80 GB H100 GPU across multiple model families and tasks. Our code is available at: github.com/Jichao2357/TACO_optimizer . 1 Introduction Full-parameter fine-tuning adapts all model weights and remains a strong baseline for transferring large language models (LLMs) to downstream tasks ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ; Hu et al., 2021 ) ; however, it often suffers from memory overhead. For instance, a 13B-parameter model occupies roughly 26 GB of memory in BF16 before allocating any training state. During AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) fine-tuning, the two FP32 moment buffers add another ∼ \sim 104 GB of memory. At the same time, gradients contribute ∼ \sim 26 GB, yielding roughly 156 GB before accounting for activations, temporary workspaces, or an optional FP32 master copy; see the Pareto frontier memory-accuracy trade-off graph in Figure 1 . Thus, at this scale, AdamW’s persistent optimizer states alone require roughly 4 × 4	imes the BF16 parameter memory. Several memory-efficient first-order optimizers reduce this overhead while retaining backpropagation, including state-quantizers (AdamW8bit quantizes optimizer states ( Dettmers et al., 2021 ) ; FlashAdamW combines 8-bit optimizer states with a compact master-weight representation ( Gonzalez Ortiz et al., 2026 ) ), factorized second moment methods (Adafactor uses factorized second-moment estimates ( Shazeer and Stern, 2018 ) ), and low-rank gradient methods (GaLore projects gradients and optimizer states into a low-rank subspace ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , and APOLLO-Mini uses a rank-1 subspace to estimate adaptive scaling factors ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) ). In contrast, zeroth-order (ZO) methods avoid backpropagation and approach inference-level memory by estimating updates from forward evaluations ( Bergou et al., 2020 ; Bibi et al., 2020 ; Gorbunov et al., 2020 ; Cai et al., 2021 ; Malladi et al., 2023 ; Boucherouite et al., 2024 ) . Recent variants incorporate low-rank subspaces or curvature information to improve query efficiency ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) , but still require additional forward queries. The recently introduced Muon optimizer ( Jordan, 2024 ; Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024 ; Shah et al., 2025 ) asks a different question: what steepest-descent direction under a matrix geometry makes the update useful? Muon treats two-dimensional weights as matrices, retains a single momentum matrix, and orthogonalizes it to approximate a steepest-descent step under spectral geometry . This reduces optimizer memory relative to AdamW, although Muon’s state remains dense. Additionally, switching an AdamW-pretrained model to Muon during fine-tuning can degrade performance, a phenomenon called optimizer mismatch that is attributed to the different update geometries and implicit biases of the two optimizers ( Qu et al., 2026 ) . Zeroth-Order Muon (ZO-Muon) ( Lang et al., 2026 ) improves query efficiency, but as a zeroth-order method, it requires additional forward evaluations. Sequential evaluation for ZO methods can keep memory close to inference, but the additional function evaluations can increase computational and communication overhead, especially in distributed training or with larger batches. Thus, existing approaches, including Muon, expose a fundamental trade-off between the memory footprint of first-order training and the optimization efficiency of standard gradients, prompting a natural question: Can full-parameter fine-tuning retain first-order information and competitive wall-clock efficiency while making persistent optimizer-state memory nearly negligible? Figure 1: Performance–memory overview of TACO and other optimizers. Left: Pareto frontier memory-accuracy trade-off for fine-tuning OPT-13B on the SST-2 dataset on an 80 GB H100 GPU. TACO lies at the low-memory end of the Pareto frontier, achieving 94.22% accuracy with 27.54 GB of peak training memory. The dashed line connects the Pareto-optimal methods. The vertical line marks the 80 GB H100 memory limit. Adam achieves 95.3% accuracy with 254.8 GB of peak memory. Right: Peak GPU memory decomposition of TACO on OPT-30B across 8 downstream tasks. The bars show model state, optimizer state, and other transient memory across all eight downstream tasks. TACO’s optimizer state occupies only 0.267 GB, less than 0.5% of peak memory on each task, while the transient memory accounts for the variation across tasks. To answer this, we propose TACO , a T ernary A bsolute-max C olumn-wise O ne-sparse optimizer. Using the same operator-norm steepest-descent viewpoint as Muon, TACO is not just another memory-efficient optimizer ; TACO’s conceptual centerpiece is an optimization geometry whose exact steepest-descent direction has extreme structural sparsity. Under a dimension-normalized → 1 1\!	o\!1 operator norm, the corresponding dual geometry makes the steepest-descent direction separable across columns, and each column selects the sign of its largest-magnitude gradient coordinate. Thus, an m × n m	imes n update contains at most n n nonzeros. Although the TACO steepest-descent direction is one-sparse per column, minibatch gradients can make the selected coordinates unstable across training. A conventional dense gradient history can stabilize coordinate selection but erodes the memory advantage. TACO instead retains only a small, low-precision set of dynamic gradient heavy hitters per column. This sparse gradient history keeps persistent optimizer-state memory negligible even as model size grows. For example, TACO can fine-tune OPT-30B on a single 80 GB H100 GPU, with peak GPU memory of 62.5 GB on SST-2, 64.7 GB on RTE, and 68.1 GB on BoolQ; see Peak GPU memory decomposition in Figure 1 . Adam does not fit this model on a single H100 80 GB GPU. Across our study, TACO enables full-parameter fine-tuning of models up to 32B parameters on a single 80 GB H100 and transfers across multiple model families and tasks. Taken together, our main contributions are: ( i ) Geometry-induced sparse optimization. We propose TACO, a new first-order optimizer for memory-efficient full-parameter LLM fine-tuning. TACO is derived from the exact steepest-descent solution under a dimension-normalized → 1 1\!	o\!1 operator norm, whose geometry naturally yields a ternary, column-wise Top-1 update. Thus, TACO’s sparsity is intrinsic to its optimization geometry rather than imposed by post-hoc gradient sparsification; see Section 3 . ( ii ) Convergence and fine-tuning theory. We prove that vanilla TACO reaches an ε \varepsilon -stationary point in 𝒪 ⁡ ( ε − 2 ) \mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}) iterations under standard smoothness assumptions. We further show that, in our theoretical setting, TACO shares the continuation geometry and limiting solution of an Adam proxy while differing from Muon, and satisfies standard μ \mu P spectral scaling under balanced winner counts. These results connect TACO to optimizer mismatch and the learning rate transfer problem; see Sections 3 and 4 . ( iii ) TACO-specific memory-efficient design. TACO does not require an accurate dense model of the gradient history, but only enough information to recover the dominant coordinate in each column. Exploiting this structure, we develop a practical implementation based on dynamic FP8 sparse gradient histories and immediate gradient processing, reducing persistent state from 𝒪 ⁡ ( m ​ n ) \mathcal{O}(mn) to 𝒪 ⁡ ( n ) \mathcal{O}(n) while retaining first-order gradients and the column-wise Top-1 update; see Section 5 . ( iv ) Empirical validation at scale. We evaluate TACO across model scales, architectures, and downstream tasks. TACO achieves competitive task performance with substantially reduced training memory, enables full-parameter fine-tuning of OPT-30B and Qwen3-32B on a single 80 GB H100 GPU, and transfers across OPT, Qwen3, Pythia, Llama, and Mistral model families. Ablations further characterize the roles of the gradient history EMA decay factor, heavy hitter threshold, update sparsity, and optimizer step budget; see Section 6 . 2 Related Work Zeroth-order optimization has become a practical way to reduce the memory cost of LLM fine-tuning. These methods construct an update direction from the change in loss under a parameter perturbation. MeZO applies this idea by regenerating its perturbations in place using a seeding trick ( Malladi et al., 2023 ) . Sparse MeZO reduces the number of perturbed parameters, preserving sparsity ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . ZO-Muon projects the estimated gradient into a lower-dimensional subspace and applies polar orthogonalization to recover more useful structure from the noisy estimate ( Lang et al., 2026 ) . HiZOO instead incorporates diagonal Hessian information into zeroth-order optimization, using curvature-aware preconditioning to improve convergence ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) . Memory-efficient first-order optimization methods retain backpropagation while reducing parameter-associated training state. Adafactor represents second moments using row and column factors ( Shazeer and Stern, 2018 ) , while CAME adds a confidence-guided correction to improve the stability of this representation ( Luo et al., 2023 ) . Alternatively, 8-bit Adam uses block-wise quantization to store optimizer statistics at lower precision ( Dettmers et al., 2021 ) . FlashOptim combines quantized optimizer states with a compact master-weight representation and provides FlashAdamW as a drop-in AdamW variant ( Gonzalez Ortiz et al., 2026 ) . GaLore projects gradients and optimizer states into a lower-dimensional space ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , whereas APOLLO approximates adaptive gradient scaling through a random low-rank auxiliary space; its APOLLO-Mini variant reduces this space to rank one and applies tensor-wise scaling ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) . Operator-norm and linear-minimization-oracle (LMO) optimization. Bernstein and Newhouse (2024) formulate matrix optimization as steepest-descent under operator norms and characterize the → p 1\!	o\!p family through maximum column norms. Pethick et al. (2025) develop a stochastic LMO framework and instantiate it with layer-aware operator geometries in Scion. Sign-based methods. In gradient compression, TernGrad maps gradient values to { − 1 , 0 , + 1 } \{-1,0,+1\} to reduce the communication bottleneck in distributed training ( Wen et al., 2017 ) , while signSGD retains only the coordinate-wise gradient signs ( Bernstein et al., 2018 ) ; see GRACE ( Xu et al., 2021 ) , a compressed communication framework that places these methods under one umbrella. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.02198 (cs) [Submitted on 1 Oct 2026] Title: FERPO: Forward Entropy-Regularized Policy Optimization Authors: Sebastian Sanokowski , Alireza Sarmadi , Majid Khadiv View a PDF of the paper titled FERPO: Forward Entropy-Regularized Policy Optimization, by Sebastian Sanokowski and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Several state-of-the-art methods for online reinforcement learning in continuous control improve policies using action gradients of a learned critic. However, critics are typically trained to predict returns, and accurate value predictions do not necessarily yield accurate action derivatives, potentially leading to unreliable policy updates. We propose Forward Entropy-Regularized Policy Optimization (FERPO), an on-policy maximum entropy reinforcement learning algorithm that performs policy improvement using critic values without differentiating the critic with respect to actions. FERPO derives an optimal target action distribution from a policy-improvement objective regularized by entropy and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. We then fit the actor to this target by minimizing a forward-KL objective, estimated using self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS) with actions drawn from the rollout policy. By limiting the target distribution's deviation from the rollout policy, the KL regularization helps keep these importance weights well behaved. In contrast to reverse-KL objectives, which can favor a subset of the target distribution's modes, the forward-KL objective encourages coverage of multiple high-value modes and thereby promotes exploration. Experiments and ablations on MuJoCo Playground and ManiSkill show competitive performance and sample-efficiency gains. Computational benchmarks also demonstrate faster actor updates than Relative Entropy Pathwise Policy Optimization (REPPO). FERPO: Forward Entropy-Regularized Policy Optimization Sebastian Sanokowski Affiliation: Applied and Theoretical Aspects of Robot Intelligence (ATARI) Lab Alireza Sarmadi Affiliation: Munich Institute of Robotics and Machine Intelligence (MIRMI) Majid Khadiv Affiliation: Technical University of Munich Abstract Several state-of-the-art methods for online reinforcement learning in continuous control improve policies using action gradients of a learned critic. However, critics are typically trained to predict returns, and accurate value predictions do not necessarily yield accurate action derivatives, potentially leading to unreliable policy updates. We propose Forward Entropy-Regularized Policy Optimization (FERPO), an on-policy maximum entropy reinforcement learning algorithm that performs policy improvement using critic values without differentiating the critic with respect to actions. FERPO derives an optimal target action distribution from a policy-improvement objective regularized by entropy and Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence. We then fit the actor to this target by minimizing a forward-KL objective, estimated using self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS) with actions drawn from the rollout policy. By limiting the target distribution’s deviation from the rollout policy, the KL regularization helps keep these importance weights well behaved. In contrast to reverse-KL objectives, which can favor a subset of the target distribution’s modes, the forward-KL objective encourages coverage of multiple high-value modes and thereby promotes exploration. Experiments and ablations on MuJoCo Playground and ManiSkill show competitive performance and sample-efficiency gains. Computational benchmarks also demonstrate faster actor updates than Relative Entropy Pathwise Policy Optimization (REPPO). Our implementation is publicly available. 1 1 1 Code: https://github.com/Atarilab/FERPO . 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) learns policies through interaction to maximize cumulative reward. Its successes range from game playing ( ? ) to autonomous drone racing ( ? ) and robot locomotion ( ? ). In robotics, massively parallel simulation has accelerated on-policy learning by collecting trajectories from thousands of environments simultaneously. This has enabled rapid policy training and successful transfer from simulation to physical robots ( ?? ). These advances make efficient and reliable policy improvement central to scaling online robot learning. Relative Entropy Pathwise Policy Optimization (REPPO; ? ) is a recent state-of-the-art on-policy method for this setting. It learns a soft action-value critic from on-policy trajectories and improves the actor by differentiating the critic with respect to actions, while limiting policy changes relative to the rollout policy. This makes pathwise actor updates compatible with massively parallel on-policy learning. However, standard critic training supervises values, whereas these actor updates require accurate action derivatives. Accurate value predictions do not necessarily imply accurate derivatives: critic-gradient error can bias policy improvement ( ? ), and learned action gradients can show poor directional agreement with rollout-based estimates ( ? ). In on-policy learning, biased gradients can also interact with changing data distributions and destabilize training ( ? ). These limitations motivate policy improvement that uses critic values without requiring their action derivatives. We derive the optimal target distribution for a standard RL policy-improvement objective with entropy and Kullback–Leibler (KL) regularization. Making this target explicit lets us replace reverse-KL projection by forward-KL fitting, which encourages coverage of target modes ( ? ). The KL trust region keeps the target close to the rollout policy, helping control importance-weight concentration, as in recent diffusion and normalizing flow based sampling methods ( ?? ). We introduce Forward Entropy-Regularized Policy Optimization (FERPO), which applies this construction to on-policy learning. Its actor update uses critic values without differentiating the critic with respect to actions. Our contributions are: • An on-policy actor update that uses critic values to construct a regularized target action distribution and fits the actor to this target using forward KL, without differentiating the critic with respect to actions (Section 3.1 ). • A practical estimator using self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS), with Lagrange multipliers that regulate policy entropy and importance-weight concentration through normalized effective sample size (ESS) (Sections 3.1 and 3.2 ). • An evaluation on ManiSkill and MuJoCo Playground demonstrating competitive performance and sample-efficiency gains (Section 5.4 ), supported by ablations (Section 5.3 ) and computational benchmarks showing faster actor updates than REPPO (Section 5.2 ). • Cached actor updates that reduce computation, and a state-value extension based on one-step simulation, with promising results on AcrobotSwingupSparse (Section 5.3 ). 2 Problem Description Maximum-entropy reinforcement learning. FERPO: Forward Entropy-Regularized Policy Optimization Sebastian Sanokowski Affiliation: Applied and Theoretical Aspects of Robot Intelligence (ATARI) Lab Alireza Sarmadi Affiliation: Munich Institute of Robotics and Machine Intelligence (MIRMI) Majid Khadiv Affiliation: Technical University of Munich Abstract Several state-of-the-art methods for online reinforcement learning in continuous control improve policies using action gradients of a learned critic. However, critics are typically trained to predict returns, and accurate value predictions do not necessarily yield accurate action derivatives, potentially leading to unreliable policy updates. We propose Forward Entropy-Regularized Policy Optimization (FERPO), an on-policy maximum entropy reinforcement learning algorithm that performs policy improvement using critic values without differentiating the critic with respect to actions. FERPO derives an optimal target action distribution from a policy-improvement objective regularized by entropy and Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence. We then fit the actor to this target by minimizing a forward-KL objective, estimated using self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS) with actions drawn from the rollout policy. By limiting the target distribution’s deviation from the rollout policy, the KL regularization helps keep these importance weights well behaved. In contrast to reverse-KL objectives, which can favor a subset of the target distribution’s modes, the forward-KL objective encourages coverage of multiple high-value modes and thereby promotes exploration. Experiments and ablations on MuJoCo Playground and ManiSkill show competitive performance and sample-efficiency gains. Computational benchmarks also demonstrate faster actor updates than Relative Entropy Pathwise Policy Optimization (REPPO). Our implementation is publicly available. 1 1 1 Code: https://github.com/Atarilab/FERPO . 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) learns policies through interaction to maximize cumulative reward. Its successes range from game playing ( ? ) to autonomous drone racing ( ? ) and robot locomotion ( ? ). In robotics, massively parallel simulation has accelerated on-policy learning by collecting trajectories from thousands of environments simultaneously. This has enabled rapid policy training and successful transfer from simulation to physical robots ( ?? ). These advances make efficient and reliable policy improvement central to scaling online robot learning. Relative Entropy Pathwise Policy Optimization (REPPO; ? ) is a recent state-of-the-art on-policy method for this setting. It learns a soft action-value critic from on-policy trajectories and improves the actor by differentiating the critic with respect to actions, while limiting policy changes relative to the rollout policy. This makes pathwise actor updates compatible with massively parallel on-policy learning. However, standard critic training supervises values, whereas these actor updates require accurate action derivatives. Accurate value predictions do not necessarily imply accurate derivatives: critic-gradient error can bias policy improvement ( ? ), and learned action gradients can show poor directional agreement with rollout-based estimates ( ? ). In on-policy learning, biased gradients can also interact with changing data distributions and destabilize training ( ? ). These limitations motivate policy improvement that uses critic values without requiring their action derivatives. We derive the optimal target distribution for a standard RL policy-improvement objective with entropy and Kullback–Leibler (KL) regularization. Making this target explicit lets us replace reverse-KL projection by forward-KL fitting, which encourages coverage of target modes ( ? ). The KL trust region keeps the target close to the rollout policy, helping control importance-weight concentration, as in recent diffusion and normalizing flow based sampling methods ( ?? ). We introduce Forward Entropy-Regularized Policy Optimization (FERPO), which applies this construction to on-policy learning. Its actor update uses critic values without differentiating the critic with respect to actions. Our contributions are: • An on-policy actor update that uses critic values to construct a regularized target action distribution and fits the actor to this target using forward KL, without differentiating the critic with respect to actions (Section 3.1 ). • A practical estimator using self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS), with Lagrange multipliers that regulate policy entropy and importance-weight concentration through normalized effective sample size (ESS) (Sections 3.1 and 3.2 ). • An evaluation on ManiSkill and MuJoCo Playground demonstrating competitive performance and sample-efficiency gains (Section 5.4 ), supported by ablations (Section 5.3 ) and computational benchmarks showing faster actor updates than REPPO (Section 5.2 ). • Cached actor updates that reduce computation, and a state-value extension based on one-step simulation, with promising results on AcrobotSwingupSparse (Section 5.3 ). 2 Problem Description Maximum-entropy reinforcement learning. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.02191 (cs) [Submitted on 1 Oct 2026] Title: The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models Authors: Shuo Xing , Zilin Dai , Chengyuan Qian , Fangzhou Lin , Wenjing Chen , Ping He , Pan Lu , Alvaro Velasquez , Mohit Bansal , Zhengzhong Tu View a PDF of the paper titled The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models, by Shuo Xing and 9 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated striking capabilities on frontier mathematical problems, it remains unclear whether they possess the structural mathematical understanding underlying their solutions. In this paper, we take a first step toward systematically studying mathematical understanding in LLMs, from diagnosing its distinct capabilities to leveraging these findings to improve post-training. First, we introduce the notion of Mathematical Primitive to probe structural mathematical understanding and propose \hlei{}, a novel benchmark that evaluates mathematical reasoning along four distinct dimensions: Discovery, Generation, Digestion, and Execution. Second, our systematic diagnosis shows that solution accuracy masks distinct capability profiles, primitives unlock substantial latent execution capacity, and Discovery is the dominant bottleneck in mathematical reasoning. Our post-training analysis further shows that discovery-limited failures are particularly amenable to repair. Finally, building on these findings, we introduce \abs{}, a primitive-privileged self-distillation framework that selectively transfers primitive-guided reasoning into the student model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that \abs{} consistently improves mathematical reasoning over baselines across model scales and challenging benchmarks. Email: {shuoxing,tzz}@tamu.edu ˜Model & Code: https://taco-group.github.io/Math-Primitive/ Affiliation: Texas A&M University Abstract While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated striking capabilities on frontier mathematical problems, it remains unclear whether they possess the structural mathematical understanding underlying their solutions. In this paper, we take a first step toward systematically studying mathematical understanding in LLMs, from diagnosing its distinct capabilities to leveraging these findings to improve post-training. First, we introduce the notion of Mathematical Primitive to probe structural mathematical understanding and propose Prim , a novel benchmark that evaluates mathematical reasoning along four distinct dimensions: Discovery, Generation, Digestion, and Execution. Second, our systematic diagnosis shows that solution accuracy masks distinct capability profiles, primitives unlock substantial latent execution capacity, and Discovery is the dominant bottleneck in mathematical reasoning. Our post-training analysis further shows that discovery-limited failures are particularly amenable to repair. Finally, building on these findings, we introduce Absorb , a primitive-privileged self-distillation framework that selectively transfers primitive-guided reasoning into the student model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Absorb consistently improves mathematical reasoning over baselines across model scales and challenging benchmarks. 1 Introduction Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have driven rapid progress in mathematical problem solving, with frontier models increasingly capable of tackling research-level questions and, in several recent cases, resolving or making substantive progress on long-standing open problems ( OpenAI, 2026d ; OpenAI, 2026c ; Claude, 2026 ; Bubeck et al., 2025 ; Jang and Ryu, 2025 ) . Yet these striking successes leave unresolved a more foundational question: what models actually understand about the problems they solve and the mathematical content of the solutions they produce. Successful problem solving does not necessarily imply such understanding: models may arrive at correct answers through specious deductions ( Boye and Moell, 2025 ) , while conversely identifying sound high-level proof structures yet failing in low-level technical execution ( Lu et al., 2024 ; Qin et al., 2025 ) . Existing works provide limited insight into this disconnect, as mathematical reasoning is still assessed primarily through outcome-level metrics such as final-answer accuracy or formal proof verifiability, obscuring whether success reflects the discovery of the mathematical structure needed for a solution or merely the successful execution of a derivation. Understanding mathematical reasoning therefore requires more than verifying that a derivation is correct; it requires exposing the ideas that organize the argument—why it works, which components are essential, and what can be generalized or reused. This need becomes increasingly salient as LLM-generated proofs grow in scale and complexity: lengthy chains of valid steps may establish correctness while leaving the underlying mathematical structure difficult to identify. Recent work has begun to emphasize precisely these aspects of mathematical reasoning, calling for representations that reveal the motivation, structure, and key ideas underlying an argument rather than only its final outcome ( Frieder et al., 2024 ) . In his ICM 2026 lecture, Terence Tao similarly highlighted the importance of making machine-generated mathematics conceptually digestible ( Tao, 2026 ) , warning that optimizing primarily for formal correctness risks producing an increasing volume of valid but opaque proofs without a corresponding increase in mathematical understanding. For LLMs, this perspective shifts the focus from merely producing valid proofs to determining whether the structural knowledge organizing those proofs is actually accessible to the model. In this paper, we systematically study structural mathematical understanding in LLMs, as illustrated in Figure 1 : the ability to identify the compact, load-bearing mathematical structure that explains why a solution works , distinct from the procedural ability to generate the derivation itself. We operationalize this notion through the Mathematical Primitive , a concise, non-procedural representation of the foundational idea organizing a solution, and introduce Prim , a benchmark spanning four complementary dimensions: Discovery, Generation, Digestion, and Execution. Our diagnosis reveals that ❶ similar solving accuracy can mask markedly different capability profiles , ❷ correct primitives unlock substantial latent execution capacity , and, most importantly, ❸ independent Discovery is the dominant bottleneck to mathematical reasoning. We further find that discovery-limited failures are substantially more amenable to post-training, but existing methods can introduce regressions on problems the model already solves. Motivated by these findings, we introduce Absorb , a post-training paradigm that uses Mathematical Primitives as privileged information and a bounded override mechanism to selectively transfer their guidance into the student’s reasoning process, enabling primitive-guided reasoning to be internalized without access to primitives at inference time. Our main contributions are as follows: • Benchmarking structural mathematical understanding. We introduce the notion of Mathematical Primitive and propose Prim , a benchmark that evaluates mathematical reasoning across four complementary dimensions: Discovery, Generation, Digestion, and Execution. • Systematic Diagnosis. Our analysis reveals distinct capability profiles hidden by answer accuracy, substantial latent execution capacity unlocked by correct primitives, and independent Discovery as the dominant bottleneck in mathematical reasoning. We further show that discovery-limited failures are substantially more amenable to post-training. • Internalizing primitive-guided reasoning. Building on these findings, we introduce Absorb , a primitive-privileged post-training paradigm that selectively transfers primitive-guided reasoning into the student model. Across multiple model scales and challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks, Absorb consistently improves average performance by 2.42 2.42 – 4.48 4.48 points. Figure 1: Diagnosing and internalizing mathematical primitives. We introduce Mathematical Primitives to probe structural mathematical understanding in LLMs across four dimensions: Discovery, Generation, Digestion, and Execution. Our diagnosis further motivates Absorb , which selectively transfers primitive-guided reasoning into the student without requiring primitives at inference time. 2 Mathematical Primitives as Structural Understanding Rather than viewing mathematical problem solving as a sequence of steps, we separate structural mathematical understanding from procedural execution . We formalize the distinction through the Mathematical Primitive (§ 2.1 ) and introduce Prim , a benchmark that evaluates LLM mathematical reasoning across four dimensions: Generation, Discovery, Digestion, and Execution (§ 2.3 ). 2.1 Mathematical Primitive A mathematical solution often begins before the first line of a proof, when an opaque problem is recognized through the structure that makes it solvable. We term this load-bearing structural understanding the Mathematical Primitive (Definition 1 ). Unlike generic advice such as use “induction” or “apply a theorem”, a primitive identifies the structural property that makes such a strategy applicable. It therefore serves as an intermediate reasoning object between problem understanding and procedural solution construction. Definition 1 (Mathematical Primitive) . For a mathematical problem, a primitive is the essential conceptual observation that reveals why the problem can be solved. It captures the latent mathematical structure shared by the problem and its solution, such as an invariant, a theorem condition, a representation, a reduction, or a reformulation. A primitive should be concise , problem-specific , and explanatory : it must make clear what property is being exploited and how that property unlocks the solution. It is not a routine calculation, a piece of generic advice, or a full proof. 2.2 Four Dimensions of Mathematical Understanding Taking the mathematical primitive as the fundamental concept of structural understanding, we systematically decompose mathematical reasoning into four complementary dimensions. Let x x denote the input problem, p p the corresponding mathematical primitive, y y a complete proof or solution, and π \pi an LLM solver. The four dimensions are defined as follows: • Discovery ( π ⁡ ( x ) → p ^ \pi(x)\rightarrow\hat{p} ) measures whether the model can independently identify the load-bearing mathematical primitive from the input problem alone. • Generation ( π ⁡ ( x ) → y ^ \pi(x)\rightarrow\hat{y} ) evaluates whether the model can solve the problem directly under zero-shot CoT prompting, with performance measured by exact match on the final answer. • Digestion ( π ⁡ ( x , y ) → p ^ \pi(x,y)\rightarrow\hat{p} ) instead provides the model with a complete correct solution and asks it to extract the mathematical primitive underlying the derivation, measuring whether the model can identify the underlying structure once a valid reasoning trajectory is exposed. • Execution ( π ⁡ ( x , p ) → y ^ \pi(x,p)\rightarrow\hat{y} ) conditions the solver on the mathematical primitive and evaluates whether it can successfully solve the problem once the relevant structure is explicitly provided. Both Discovery and Digestion are evaluated using the scoring protocol introduced in § 2.3 . 2.3 The Prim Benchmark Data Curation. We build on Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE) ( Center for AI Safety et al., 2026 ) , focusing on its mathematics, text-only, free-form subset with exactMatch evaluation. To reduce annotation noise in the original benchmark, we draw from the HLE-Verified release ( Zhai et al., 2026 ) , retaining its Gold and Revision subsets, from which we randomly sample 200 200 problems. For each problem, GPT-5.4-High generates an initial primitive annotation conditioned on the problem, reference answer, and gold rationale, following Definition 1 . Three human experts with graduate-level training in mathematics independently review the primitive and verify the validity of the problem, answer, and rationale. This process excludes 18 18 unsuitable problems, yielding a final evaluation set of 182 182 . Further curation and annotation details are provided in Appendix A.1 . Primitive Scoring. We evaluate each predicted primitive against the human-annotated gold primitive, using the reference solution only to recognize mathematically equivalent formulations. To account for different forms of mathematical structure, each problem is assigned to one of three primitive families, including Recast , Witness , and Argument , with full definitions provided in Appendix A.2 . Our scoring rubric evaluates three aspects of a predicted primitive: V V determines whether the response constitutes a valid primitive, σ gate \sigma_{\text{gate}} measures whether it identifies the essential mathematical structure, and σ mech \sigma_{\text{mech}} measures whether it explains how that structure enables the solution. We define Score = V ⋅ σ gate ⋅ ( 0.6 + 0.4 ⋅ σ mech ) , PrimitiveAcc = 𝟏 [ Score ≥ τ ] , \displaystyle\mathrm{Score}=V\cdot\sigma_{\text{gate}}\cdot\big(0.6+0.4\cdot\sigma_{\text{mech}}\big),\quad\mathrm{PrimitiveAcc}=\mathbf{1}\left[\mathrm{Score}\geq\tau\right], with τ = 0.8 \tau=0.8 . This formulation treats validity and structural identification as necessary conditions, while using mechanism quality to refine the score. Further details are provided in Appendix A.3 . 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning In this section, we conduct an empirical study of a diverse set of LLMs, including both open- and closed-source models, on Prim . Moving beyond standard answer correctness, our evaluation systematically disentangles procedural execution from structural understanding. We report model performance across four dimensions: Generation , Discovery , Digestion , and Execution , following the evaluation protocol described in § 2.3 . The main results are summarized in Table 3.1 . 3.1 Evaluation Setup Model Discovery Generation Digestion Dig . − Disc . \mathrm{Dig.}-\mathrm{Disc.} Execution Exec . − Gen . \mathrm{Exec.}-\mathrm{Gen.} [0pt][0pt] OpenAI gpt-5.4 82.42 82.42 67.03 67.03 100.00 100.00 (+17.58) 86.81 86.81 (+19.78) gpt-5.4-mini 59.34 59.34 50.55 50.55 97.80 97.80 (+38.46) 71.98 71.98 (+21.43) gpt-5.4-nano 41.76 41.76 44.51 44.51 97.25 97.25 (+55.49) 68.68 68.68 (+24.17) gpt-oss-20B 34.62 34.62 43.41 43.41 91.21 91.21 (+56.59) 60.99 60.99 (+17.58) [0pt][0pt] Qwen Qwen3.6-27B 24.73 24.73 52.75 52.75 92.31 92.31 (+67.58) 78.57 78.57 (+25.82) Qwen3.5-27B 28.57 28.57 47.80 47.80 93.41 93.41 (+64.84) 71.98 71.98 (+24.18) Qwen3.5-9B 13.19 13.19 38.46 38.46 79.67 79.67 (+66.48) 61.54 61.54 (+23.08) Qwen3.5-4B 6.59 6.59 26.37 26.37 70.88 70.88 (+64.29) 56.04 56.04 (+29.67) [0pt][0pt] DeepSeek-R1 Distill R1-0528-8B 6.59 6.59 17.03 17.03 68.68 68.68 (+62.09) 39.56 39.56 (+22.53) R1-Distill-32B 6.04 6.04 18.13 18.13 65.38 65.38 (+59.34) 43.41 43.41 (+25.28) R1-Distill-14B 4.40 4.40 15.93 15.93 67.03 67.03 (+62.63) 39.01 39.01 (+23.08) R1-Distill-7B 7.14 7.14 13.19 13.19 48.90 48.90 (+41.76) 32.42 32.42 (+19.23) Table 1: Overall performance on the four dimensions of Prim . Detailed results are presented in Table B.3.1 in Appendix B.3 . We evaluate 12 models spanning three lineages and a broad capability range. The OpenAI lineage includes the closed-source GPT-5.4 ( OpenAI, 2026b ) , GPT-5.4-Mini ( OpenAI, 2026a ) , and GPT-5.4-Nano ( OpenAI, 2026a ) , alongside the open-weight GPT-OSS-20B ( OpenAI, 2025 ) . The Qwen lineage comprises Qwen-3.6-27B ( Qwen Team, 2026b ) and Qwen-3.5-{27B, 9B, 4B} ( Qwen Team, 2026a ) . The DeepSeek lineage features DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-{32B, 14B, 7B} ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) . We use high reasoning effort when available and a maximum generation budget of 120k tokens per problem. 3.2 Results Analysis Table 3.1 presents the comprehensive evaluation results of all models on Prim . Performance in the Discovery and Digestion dimensions is assessed by the model’s capacity to isolate the underlying mathematical primitive, utilizing the scoring protocol detailed in § 2.3 . Meanwhile, Generation and Execution are evaluated based on standard final-answer accuracy, following the HLE benchmark ( Center for AI Safety et al., 2026 ) . Further details on the diagnostic evaluation and additional analyses are provided in Appendix B . Figure 2: Joint composition of Generation and Discovery outcomes across models. Finding 1: Answer accuracy masks distinct capability profiles. Final-answer accuracy conflates structural discovery with downstream execution. As shown in Figure 2 , Discovery and Generation are positively associated overall, yet models with similar solving accuracy can exhibit sharply different structural capabilities. For example, Qwen3.6-27B and gpt-5.4-mini achieve comparable Generation performance, while differing by over 30 30 percentage points in Discovery. Conversely, GPT-5.4 achieves substantially higher Discovery than Generation. The problem-level decomposition in Figure 2 reveals similarly distinct profiles across model families. The OpenAI lineage is more primitive-forward , with successful Generation frequently accompanied by correct Discovery and a substantial fraction of cases with correct Discovery but failed Generation ( D + ​ G − D^{+}G^{-} ). In contrast, Qwen exhibits more cases with failed Discovery but successful Generation ( D − ​ G + D^{-}G^{+} ), despite competitive Generation performance. The DeepSeek-R1 distilled models are more heavily concentrated in joint Discovery–Generation failures. Thus, similar top-line accuracy can arise from markedly different underlying capability profiles. Figure 3: Discovery versus Generation across all evaluated models on Prim . Qualitative analysis further clarifies these asymmetries. For gpt-5.4, D + ​ G − D^{+}G^{-} cases primarily reflect two post-primitive failure modes: ❶ technical knowledge gaps , where the correct structure is identified but a required lemma, theorem condition, or domain-specific fact is missing; and ❷ procedural execution failures , such as algebraic errors, missed edge cases, or unresolved logical gaps. For Qwen3.6-27B, among D − ​ G + D^{-}G^{+} cases, the decisive structural idea often emerges after an initial attempt without using it, typically around one quarter into the reasoning trace; in most remaining cases it appears at the outset, and only rarely is it absent entirely. The corresponding cold Discovery output often captures a partial form of the correct idea but misses its decisive component. Together with the longer reasoning traces in Figure 12 , this pattern is consistent with a more grind-first profile, where the relevant structure tends to emerge during extended procedural exploration rather than being isolated before execution. Finding 2: Correct primitives unlock latent execution capacity. To examine whether models possess downstream capabilities that are not realized during direct Generation, we evaluate Execution when the correct Mathematical Primitive is explicitly provided. As shown in Table 3.1 , primitive guidance improves performance by 17.58 17.58 to 29.67 29.67 percentage points across all 12 models. Notably, under the same primitive-guided setting, the Qwen models achieve Execution performance competitive with the closed-source gpt-5.4 variants despite substantially weaker Discovery. This gap shows that difficulty independently identifying the relevant mathematical structure can coexist with strong downstream problem-solving capability once that structure is available. More broadly, these gains indicate that many Generation failures mask downstream solving capacity that models can successfully exercise when the relevant mathematical structure is supplied. Detailed results are presented in Table B.3.3 in Appendix B.3 . We further investigate whether this rescue can be attributed simply to task decomposition or generic procedural scaffolding. Table 2 compares four intervention settings. Conditioning the model on its own generated primitive provides little benefit: it yields only a marginal gain for gpt-5.4-nano and substantially degrades Qwen3.6-27B, indicating that a forced discover-then-execute decomposition alone is insufficient. We then compare two forms of external guidance generated by the same teacher model (gpt-5.4) from the problem alone: a step-by-step Teacher Plan , which serves as a procedural hint by specifying the major solution steps, and a Teacher Primitive , which is generated according to the definition of primitive. Although the Teacher Plan improves over direct Generation, the Teacher Primitive yields substantially larger gains across the evaluated models. The Gold Primitive further maximizes this effect, pushing accuracy to 71.98 % 71.98\% , 68.68 % 68.68\% , and 78.57 % 78.57\% for the representative models. This contrast provides crucial empirical validation for our premise in § 2.1 : a mathematical primitive is fundamentally distinct from, and vastly more effective than, a generic plan or hint. The rescue effect therefore cannot be attributed to task decomposition or the procedural scaffold evaluated here alone; exposing the load-bearing mathematical structure provides a substantially stronger signal for downstream reasoning. Finding 3: Independent structural discovery is the dominant bottleneck. As shown in Table 3.1 , models perform substantially better on Digestion , recovering the Mathematical Primitive from a correct solution, than on Discovery , where the same primitive must be identified from the problem alone. This asymmetry is particularly pronounced outside the strongest OpenAI models. Even models with weak Discovery can often recover the organizing primitive once the relevant reasoning is exposed through a completed solution; for instance, Qwen3.6-27B rises from 24.73% Discovery to 92.31% Digestion and R1-Distill-32B from 6.04% to 65.38%. Figure 4: Decomposition of Generation failures by Discovery ( D D ) and Execution ( E E ). Detailed results can be found in Table B.3.3 in Appendix B.3 . These results reveal a pronounced gap between retrospective recognition and prospective discovery of mathematical structure: models can often recognize the key idea once it is instantiated in a valid solution, yet struggle to identify it independently before the derivation is known. To further localize this bottleneck, we decompose Generation failures according to the joint outcomes of Discovery ( D D ) and Execution ( E E ), as shown in Figure 4 . A striking 83.6 % 83.6\% of all failures fall into the D − D^{-} regime, indicating that failed primitive discovery dominates the failure landscape. Importantly, a substantial fraction of these cases are discovery-limited failures ( D − ​ E + D^{-}E^{+} ): the model fails to identify the correct primitive independently, yet succeeds once it is supplied. This reveals that, for many failures, latent execution capacity is already present but remains inaccessible because of the upstream bottleneck in primitive discovery. 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? While our preceding diagnosis reveals the failure modes of LLMs during inference, a natural follow-up question arises: how does post-training impact these mathematical reasoning failures? Of particular interest are discovery-limited failures, which exhibit substantial room for improvement (§ 3.2 ). We hypothesize that these failures lie just at the boundary of the models’ reasoning capabilities, making them highly amenable to repair through post-training. Therefore, we utilize Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) to investigate how different failure modes uniquely respond to these post-training paradigms. Setup. Our training corpus contains 709 Mathematics Ph.D. qualifying-examination problems from 1991–2026, each paired with a human-authored proof (median length: 118 words); additional details are provided in Appendix C . We use qualifying-examination problems because their open-ended, proof-oriented nature closely matches the difficulty and structural reasoning demands of Prim . Since such problems generally lack algorithmically verifiable short answers, we focus on text-supervised post-training rather than outcome-verified methods such as RLVR. Finding 1: Answer accuracy masks distinct capability profiles. Final-answer accuracy conflates structural discovery with downstream execution. As shown in Figure 2 , Discovery and Generation are positively associated overall, yet models with similar solving accuracy can exhibit sharply different structural capabilities. For example, Qwen3.6-27B and gpt-5.4-mini achieve comparable Generation performance, while differing by over 30 30 percentage points in Discovery. Conversely, GPT-5.4 achieves substantially higher Discovery than Generation. The problem-level decomposition in Figure 2 reveals similarly distinct profiles across model families. The OpenAI lineage is more primitive-forward , with successful Generation frequently accompanied by correct Discovery and a substantial fraction of cases with correct Discovery but failed Generation ( D + ​ G − D^{+}G^{-} ). In contrast, Qwen exhibits more cases with failed Discovery but successful Generation ( D − ​ G + D^{-}G^{+} ), despite competitive Generation performance. The DeepSeek-R1 distilled models are more heavily concentrated in joint Discovery–Generation failures. Thus, similar top-line accuracy can arise from markedly different underlying capability profiles. Figure 3: Discovery versus Generation across all evaluated models on Prim . For gpt-5.4, D + ​ G − D^{+}G^{-} cases primarily reflect two post-primitive failure modes: ❶ technical knowledge gaps , where the correct structure is identified but a required lemma, theorem condition, or domain-specific fact is missing; and ❷ procedural execution failures , such as algebraic errors, missed edge cases, or unresolved logical gaps. The corresponding cold Discovery output often captures a partial form of the correct idea but misses its decisive component. This gap shows that difficulty independently identifying the relevant mathematical structure can coexist with strong downstream problem-solving capability once that structure is available. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.02202 (cs) [Submitted on 1 Oct 2026] Title: ScholarCatalyst: A Benchmark for Retrieving Papers That Inspire New Research Authors: Sohyeon Kim , Yoonho Lee , Bo Liu , Dayoon Ko , Rulin Shao , Seungone Kim , Graham Neubig , Pang Wei Koh , Aakanksha Chowdhery , Akari Asai , Omar Khattab , Yejin Choi , Gunhee Kim , Chelsea Finn View a PDF of the paper titled ScholarCatalyst: A Benchmark for Retrieving Papers That Inspire New Research, by Sohyeon Kim and 13 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: What makes great scientists great? Even as AI systems start to make progress on open problems, scientists remain far ahead of them at sensing which prior idea, buried in an ever-growing archive of research, a new problem needs. To study this skill, we draw on researchers who know firsthand which earlier work advanced their completed projects, with papers serving as pointers to the ideas within. Using our automated pipeline that makes author annotation scalable, we build ScholarCatalyst by having 184 lead authors of 207 recent computer science papers label which candidates did or could have advanced their project, each with a detailed rationale. We introduce a retrieval task with author-provided judgments: given an initial research question, retrieve these papers from only the literature available when the project began. Agentic search does no better than embedding retrieval (0.42 vs. 0.48 Recall@20) despite calling that same retriever as a tool. Even an agent built on Claude Fable 5.1, which may have seen the completed papers during training, reaches only 0.51 R@20. These results highlight the need for new training recipes that equip models with expert intuition for searching broad corpora. We envision ScholarCatalyst as a step toward scientific agents that can take a half-formed idea and point to the prior research it needs. Even as AI systems start to make progress on open problems, scientists remain far ahead of them at sensing which prior idea, buried in an ever-growing archive of research, a new problem needs. To study this skill, we draw on researchers who know firsthand which earlier work advanced their completed projects, with papers serving as pointers to the ideas within.
