We introduce a retrieval task with author-provided judgments: given an initial research question, retrieve these papers from only the literature available when the project began. Agentic search does no better than embedding retrieval (0.42 vs. 0.48 Recall@20) despite calling that same retriever as a tool. Even an agent built on Claude Fable 5.1, which may have seen the completed papers during training, reaches only 0.51 R@20. These results highlight the need for new training recipes that equip models with expert intuition for searching broad corpora. We envision ScholarCatalyst as a step toward scientific agents that can take a half-formed idea and point to the prior research it needs. \scalebox{1}[0.78]{${\color[rgb]{0.6484,0.1563,0.5313}\scriptstyle\blacklozenge}$}$\mkern1.0mu$ \scalebox{1}[0.78]{${\color[rgb]{0.6484,0.1563,0.5313}\scriptstyle\blacklozenge}$}$\mkern1.0mu$ footnotetext: Equal contribution. Contact: {sohyeon,yoonho}@stanford.edu Project Page ohmyksh.github.io/project/ScholarCatalyst Dataset huggingface.co/ScholarCatalyst Code github.com/stanford-iris-lab/ScholarCatalyst Contributors ⧫ {\color[rgb]{0.6484,0.1563,0.5313}\blacklozenge} Full list in Appendix Figure 1: ScholarCatalyst asks whether a system can retrieve prior papers that inspire progress on a research project. Such a paper may share little semantic similarity with the question yet offer an insight that advances the project ( right ), while topically related work may not ( left ). 1 Introduction To invent is to discern, to choose. — Henri Poincaré Scientific research is inherently cumulative, with each project building on previous results and ideas. Current AI systems for research mainly accelerate progress on an already well-defined subproblem, where the remaining work is closer to engineering. Deciding which existing idea a new problem should build on is still mostly left to human researchers. An insightful prior paper can turn a vague question into a well-defined problem, for instance by revealing a limitation that motivates a new direction or suggesting an approach worth adapting, thereby shaping and accelerating— catalyzing —subsequent research. Making this choice well is a defining ability of great scientists, and a critical part of what researchers call research taste . We ask whether models can make that decision through a concrete task: given an early-stage research question, find its catalyst papers , by which we mean prior papers whose ideas did or could have meaningfully advanced the project ( Figure 1 ). Evaluating this retrieval task requires ground truth about which papers were catalysts for a particular project. Published papers record the outcomes of completed projects, but the ideation that shaped them is largely undocumented, and bibliographies rarely distinguish the sources that provided non-obvious, critical insights from the broader set of cited works. Existing scientific retrieval benchmarks (Table 1 ) evaluate facet-level similarity or relevance to a stated information need ( Wadden et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Ajith et al., 2024 ; Asai et al., 2024 ) or derive positives from citation-intent annotations for queries that withhold the eventual method ( Garikaparthi et al., 2025 ) . These signals do not capture whether a retrieved paper could have inspired an early-stage project, especially when it was not cited by the eventual paper. We introduce ScholarCatalyst , a literature inspiration retrieval benchmark grounded in researchers’ firsthand knowledge of their own projects. 184 researchers who led 207 recent computer science projects verified 894 research questions as they stood before each project’s key findings, then labeled which prior papers did or could have advanced their work and explained why, including papers they had not encountered at the time. Given a question, a system must rank these papers near the top of a 191K-paper corpus restricted to work published before the project, using models whose knowledge cutoffs predate every source paper. This knowledge is rarely documented, and we collect it efficiently and at scale through an automated pipeline that only needs a paper’s arXiv ID to produce author-reviewable draft data. Because any newly published paper can become a fresh instance, the pipeline keeps ScholarCatalyst ahead of model training cutoffs and lets the benchmark grow with the literature. Across sparse, dense, and multi-vector retrievers and LLM search agents, the strongest system recovers only 48% of gold (i.e., author-credited) papers in its top 20. We find that topical similarity is a weak signal: catalyst papers are no more similar to the query than related papers the authors rejected. Every search an agent issues still goes through a similarity-based retriever, so repeated querying does not help (42% vs. 48% for the retriever alone). We also evaluate Claude Fable 5.1 as a lenient upper reference because its training data may include the source papers or secondary sources describing them, and even with this advantage it misses nearly half of the gold papers in its top 20. More broadly, our results point to the need for retrieval models with an expert-level sense of which ideas matter , and ScholarCatalyst offers a way to measure progress toward them. Table 1: Comparison with literature retrieval benchmarks. ScholarCatalyst combines queries that precede a project’s solution ( Pre-discovery query ), direct author annotation ( Author annotation ), and relevance judgment beyond what is published in the completed source paper ( Undocumented relevance ). Benchmark Relevance Pre-discovery query Author annotation Undocumented relevance Queries | 𝒬 | |\mathcal{Q}| Corpus | 𝒫 | |\mathcal{P}| SciFact ( Wadden et al., 2020 ) Claim support ✗ ✗ ✗ 1.4K 5.2K DORIS-MAE ( Wang et al., 2023 ) Multi-aspect relevance ✗ ✗ ✗ 100 100 ScholarQABench ( Asai et al., 2024 ) Claim support ✗ ✗ ✗ 2,967 45M LitSearch ( Ajith et al., 2024 ) Citation relation ✗ ✓ ✗ 597 64K MIR ( Garikaparthi et al., 2025 ) Methodological citation intent ✓ ✗ ✗ 139 4.7K ScholarCatalyst (ours) Author-judged inspiration ✓ ✓ ✓ 894 191K † LitSearch asks authors to write 246 of its 597 queries to retrieve their own papers. 2 Related Work Scientific discovery using LLMs. Accelerating science is a major opportunity for LLM-based agents, which increasingly can propose relevant hypotheses and research ideas ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Wang et al., 2024b ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . We deliberately ground our task in existing papers . Unlike a newly generated idea, which cannot be verified without running it ( Si et al., 2025 ; Si et al., 2026 ) , a published paper comes with a record of what worked, why, and where it fell short. The same grounding is what lets us collect ground truth, since authors can judge existing papers against what actually advanced their project. Existing scientific-discovery systems likewise draw on prior papers, either starting from a seed or target paper and exploiting its citation graph or metadata ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Liu et al., 2025 ) , while others search a task-specific candidate corpus constructed in advance ( Wang et al., 2024b ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Recent work studies how LLMs can generate scientific insights by combining existing ideas ( He-Yueya et al., 2026 ) , further motivating the need to evaluate which prior work agents choose to draw on. ScholarCatalyst directly addresses this evaluation gap by testing whether scientific agents can retrieve insightful prior ideas for an early-stage research question, guided by project authors’ firsthand experience of what helped their research. Scientific literature retrieval. Existing scientific retrieval benchmarks evaluate how well systems find evidence for claims ( Wadden et al., 2020 ; Wadden et al., 2022 ) , retrieve documents for specified facets ( Mysore et al., 2021 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) , and locate papers given document context or explicit information needs ( Ajith et al., 2024 ; Asai et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2025 ; Park et al., 2025 ; Shao et al., 2025 ) . Whereas existing benchmarks provide a retrieval objective that is explicit in the query, we pose an open-ended problem that requires inferring the latent scientific relevance of papers to an early-stage research idea. MIR ( Garikaparthi et al., 2025 ) comes closest, since its queries also withhold the project’s eventual method, but it derives positives from citation-intent annotations indicating methodological influence ( Lauscher et al., 2022 ) . Rather than inferring relevance from the published record, we elicit directly from paper authors otherwise undocumented data about the research process behind it, including early-stage research questions and relevance judgments. To our knowledge, ScholarCatalyst is the first scientific literature retrieval benchmark grounded in authors’ firsthand accounts of their research process. Information retrieval systems. Lexical retrievers ( Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009 ) and embedding retrievers rank corpus papers through term overlap or learned semantic similarity ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ; Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Shanbhogue et al., 2026 ) . For a given query, these methods rank the corpus once and do not adapt the search to the returned papers. Search agents use LLM reasoning to iteratively formulate queries and invoke these retrievers as tools over multiple turns, enabling more adaptive search for complex information-seeking tasks ( Yao et al., 2022 ; Jin et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . Deep research systems extend this approach with subquestion decomposition, reading, and reflection over longer horizons ( Team et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . However, these agents still access the corpus through a retriever’s top- k k candidates at each step. Recent work instead gives agents direct access to the raw corpus through terminal tools such as grep and file reads, letting the language model determine how to search and interpret documents ( Li et al., 2026 ; Sen et al., 2026 ) . Whether such agentic search approaches can retrieve prior work whose scientific inspiration is latent rather than lexically explicit remains unclear. 3 ScholarCatalyst: Evaluating Scientific Literature Retrieval with Authors’ Firsthand Accounts ScholarCatalyst evaluates whether retrieval systems can identify catalyst papers , prior work whose ideas could inspire and help advance an early stage of research. To obtain firsthand judgments about inspiration, we ask project authors which prior papers did or could have helped advance their project and why, knowledge that is largely absent from the public record. We first define the task of retrieving useful prior work, including its query types, retrieval corpus, and evaluation metrics ( Section 3.1 ). We then describe our pipeline that supports effective and efficient data collection ( Section 3.2 ) and the subsequent author validation and revision process for finalizing the benchmark instances ( Section 3.3 ). Figure 2: An example ScholarCatalyst instance. An author of the source paper S S provides a research question q q , expressed as a CoreQ or SubQ , along with positive and hard negative papers 𝒟 q + , 𝒟 q − \mathcal{D}_{q}^{+},\mathcal{D}_{q}^{-} and a rationale for these judgments. 3.1 Task Definition Given a query q q from the authors of the source paper S S , the task is to retrieve catalyst papers 𝒟 q + \smash{\mathcal{D}^{+}_{q}} from 𝒫 < S \smash{\mathcal{P}_{<S}} , where 𝒫 < S \smash{\mathcal{P}_{<S}} is a corpus containing papers published before source paper S S was completed. For each query q q , we also provide hard-negative documents, 𝒟 q − ⊂ 𝒫 < S \smash{\mathcal{D}^{-}_{q}\subset\mathcal{P}_{<S}} , which are related to q q but did not inspire the authors of S S . Each query q q is a short paragraph that reconstructs the research landscape at the outset of the project underlying the source paper S S . It describes what was known, what remained unresolved, and the open question the authors set out to answer, without revealing the eventual solution. Specifically, we consider two query types that reflect how an early-stage project develops from a broad central research question into particular subfields, with an inspiring paper potentially shaping the next step at either stage. • A core research query ( CoreQ ) asks which prior ideas could help address the project’s central research question. • A subfield-specific query ( SubQ ) approaches the same research question from a particular research subfield, asking which prior ideas could help advance the project from that perspective. Figure 2 shows an example ScholarCatalyst instance ( q , 𝒟 q + , 𝒟 q − ) (q,\smash{\mathcal{D}^{+}_{q}},\smash{\mathcal{D}^{-}_{q}}) derived from source paper S S . For each query q q , the positive paper set 𝒟 q + ⊆ 𝒫 < S \smash{\mathcal{D}^{+}_{q}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{<S}} contains papers that authors judge to offer inspiration for pursuing q q . The hard-negative set 𝒟 q − ⊆ 𝒫 < S ∖ 𝒟 q + \smash{\mathcal{D}^{-}_{q}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{<S}\setminus\mathcal{D}^{+}_{q}} contains papers that the authors reviewed and rejected. Every hard-negative paper is topically related to q q , since it was either cited in S S or ranked highly for q q by a retriever. By making the retrieval corpus 𝒫 < S \smash{\mathcal{P}_{<S}} contain only papers published before S S ( Yetisgen-Yildiz and Pratt, 2008 ; Yetisgen-Yildiz and Pratt, 2009 ; Halawi et al., 2024 ) , we approximate the literature available during the research process. We also disable external web access to prevent retrieval of subsequent writing about the project and the source paper. We evaluate retrieval performance using Recall@ N N , which measures the fraction of positive papers retrieved in the top N N results, and normalized discounted cumulative gain (nDCG@ N N ) ( Järvelin and Kekäläinen, 2002 ) , which additionally rewards higher rankings of positive papers. 3.2 Our Automated Pipeline for Efficient Data Collection We build an automated data construction pipeline that only requires a source paper’s arXiv ID and produces the materials required for author annotation. The pipeline let us collect author-validated data at scale. It also makes it easy to refresh ScholarCatalyst with newly published papers as older instances go stale due to leakage into newer models’ training data. Source-paper and corpus processing. For each source paper S S , we use the arXiv API 1 1 1 https://info.arxiv.org/help/api/index.html to obtain metadata and source files, parse the full text into a structured representation, and resolve bibliography entries to canonical scholarly records. The resulting one-hop citation graph links inline citations to the referenced papers’ metadata and abstracts. Our retrieval corpus 𝒫 \mathcal{P} contains 190,896 papers. It combines references resolved from our source papers with 181K additional arXiv papers from 2020–2024 across major computer-science categories. Scoping 𝒫 \mathcal{P} to computer science and the source papers’ publication years keeps the corpus relevant to ScholarCatalyst without indexing all of arXiv, which now exceeds 3 million articles ( arXiv, 2026 ) . We show detailed corpus statistics in Section B.2 . Pre-annotation and candidate construction. We use Gemini 3.1 Pro to generate pre-annotations from the structured source paper S S and its bibliography. These include one CoreQ , several SubQ s, and rationales explaining the proposed relevance of cited papers. We additionally retrieve uncited candidates with BM25 and Qwen3-Embedding-8B ( Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) . Gemini 3.6 Flash ( Google DeepMind, 2026b ) reranks the pooled candidates for scientific relevance, and the pipeline retains 10 candidates per query to balance coverage of potential false negatives with a manageable author-review workload. The resulting pre-annotations and candidates are loaded into a web interface for author review ( Section 3.3 ). We describe the implementation details of our pipeline in Appendix E . Figure 3: ScholarCatalyst construction process. Our automated data-collection pipeline constructs a retrieval corpus and author-review materials, including structured paper data and candidate papers ( Section 3.2 ), which authors review through our interface to validate and revise queries, judge candidate-paper relevance, and provide rationales ( Section 3.3 ). Table 2: Dataset statistics. For each query type, we report the number of queries, the average number of positive papers ( | 𝒟 q + | |\mathcal{D}^{+}_{q}| ) and hard negatives ( | 𝒟 q − | |\mathcal{D}^{-}_{q}| ), and the average query length in tokens. Query type Queries Avg. | 𝒟 q + | |\mathcal{D}^{+}_{q}| Cited / Uncited Pos. (%) Avg. | 𝒟 q − | |\mathcal{D}^{-}_{q}| Avg. Length Core Research Query 207 3.19 95.5 / 4.5 10.01 131.8 Subfield-specific Query 687 6.09 56.4 / 43.6 6.88 63.5 3.3 Collecting Relevance Supervision from Authors We collect 207 projects from 184 researchers, each describing the intellectual path behind a source paper S S in computer science (CS) and artificial intelligence (AI), published in 2025–2026. Each project contributes one CoreQ task instance and one or more SubQ task instances, each of the form ( q , 𝒟 q + , 𝒟 q − ) \bigl(q,\mathcal{D}^{+}_{q},\mathcal{D}^{-}_{q}\bigr) , together with a rationale for the relevance judgments. 1. Author recruitment. We recruit participants in two ways. We invite first authors of oral, spotlight, and award papers at major AI conferences in 2025--2026 2 2 2 ICLR 2026, ICML 2026, NeurIPS 2025, ACL 2026, CVPR 2026, CoLM 2025, and CoRL 2025. . items.raw_text: Scholar atalyst: A Benchmark for Retrieving Papers that Inspire New Research Sohyeon Kim Yoonho Lee Bo Liu Dayoon Ko Rulin Shao Affiliation: Stanford University Seoul National University University of Washington Seungone Kim Graham Neubig Pang Wei Koh Aakanksha Chowdhery Affiliation: Stanford University Seoul National University University of Washington Akari Asai Omar Khattab Yejin Choi Gunhee Kim Chelsea Finn Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Allen Institute for AI MIT Abstract What makes great scientists great? Even as AI systems start to make progress on open problems, scientists remain far ahead of them at sensing which prior idea, buried in an ever-growing archive of research, a new problem needs. To study this skill, we draw on researchers who know firsthand which earlier work advanced their completed projects, with papers serving as pointers to the ideas within. Using our automated pipeline that makes author annotation scalable, we build ScholarCatalyst by having 184 lead authors of 207 recent computer science papers label which candidates did or could have advanced their project, each with a detailed rationale. We introduce a retrieval task with author-provided judgments: given an initial research question, retrieve these papers from only the literature available when the project began. Agentic search does no better than embedding retrieval (0.42 vs. 0.48 Recall@20) despite calling that same retriever as a tool. Even an agent built on Claude Fable 5.1, which may have seen the completed papers during training, reaches only 0.51 R@20. These results highlight the need for new training recipes that equip models with expert intuition for searching broad corpora. We envision ScholarCatalyst as a step toward scientific agents that can take a half-formed idea and point to the prior research it needs. \scalebox{1}[0.78]{${\color[rgb]{0.6484,0.1563,0.5313}\scriptstyle\blacklozenge}$}$\mkern1.0mu$ \scalebox{1}[0.78]{${\color[rgb]{0.6484,0.1563,0.5313}\scriptstyle\blacklozenge}$}$\mkern1.0mu$ footnotetext: Equal contribution. Contact: {sohyeon,yoonho}@stanford.edu Project Page ohmyksh.github.io/project/ScholarCatalyst Dataset huggingface.co/ScholarCatalyst Code github.com/stanford-iris-lab/ScholarCatalyst Contributors ⧫ {\color[rgb]{0.6484,0.1563,0.5313}\blacklozenge} Full list in Appendix Figure 1: ScholarCatalyst asks whether a system can retrieve prior papers that inspire progress on a research project. Such a paper may share little semantic similarity with the question yet offer an insight that advances the project ( right ), while topically related work may not ( left ). 1 Introduction To invent is to discern, to choose. — Henri Poincaré Scientific research is inherently cumulative, with each project building on previous results and ideas. Current AI systems for research mainly accelerate progress on an already well-defined subproblem, where the remaining work is closer to engineering. Deciding which existing idea a new problem should build on is still mostly left to human researchers. An insightful prior paper can turn a vague question into a well-defined problem, for instance by revealing a limitation that motivates a new direction or suggesting an approach worth adapting, thereby shaping and accelerating— catalyzing —subsequent research. Making this choice well is a defining ability of great scientists, and a critical part of what researchers call research taste . We ask whether models can make that decision through a concrete task: given an early-stage research question, find its catalyst papers , by which we mean prior papers whose ideas did or could have meaningfully advanced the project ( Figure 1 ). Evaluating this retrieval task requires ground truth about which papers were catalysts for a particular project. Published papers record the outcomes of completed projects, but the ideation that shaped them is largely undocumented, and bibliographies rarely distinguish the sources that provided non-obvious, critical insights from the broader set of cited works. Existing scientific retrieval benchmarks (Table 1 ) evaluate facet-level similarity or relevance to a stated information need ( Wadden et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Ajith et al., 2024 ; Asai et al., 2024 ) or derive positives from citation-intent annotations for queries that withhold the eventual method ( Garikaparthi et al., 2025 ) . These signals do not capture whether a retrieved paper could have inspired an early-stage project, especially when it was not cited by the eventual paper. We introduce ScholarCatalyst , a literature inspiration retrieval benchmark grounded in researchers’ firsthand knowledge of their own projects. 184 researchers who led 207 recent computer science projects verified 894 research questions as they stood before each project’s key findings, then labeled which prior papers did or could have advanced their work and explained why, including papers they had not encountered at the time. Given a question, a system must rank these papers near the top of a 191K-paper corpus restricted to work published before the project, using models whose knowledge cutoffs predate every source paper. This knowledge is rarely documented, and we collect it efficiently and at scale through an automated pipeline that only needs a paper’s arXiv ID to produce author-reviewable draft data. Because any newly published paper can become a fresh instance, the pipeline keeps ScholarCatalyst ahead of model training cutoffs and lets the benchmark grow with the literature. Across sparse, dense, and multi-vector retrievers and LLM search agents, the strongest system recovers only 48% of gold (i.e., author-credited) papers in its top 20. We find that topical similarity is a weak signal: catalyst papers are no more similar to the query than related papers the authors rejected. Every search an agent issues still goes through a similarity-based retriever, so repeated querying does not help (42% vs. 48% for the retriever alone). We also evaluate Claude Fable 5.1 as a lenient upper reference because its training data may include the source papers or secondary sources describing them, and even with this advantage it misses nearly half of the gold papers in its top 20. More broadly, our results point to the need for retrieval models with an expert-level sense of which ideas matter , and ScholarCatalyst offers a way to measure progress toward them. Table 1: Comparison with literature retrieval benchmarks. ScholarCatalyst combines queries that precede a project’s solution ( Pre-discovery query ), direct author annotation ( Author annotation ), and relevance judgment beyond what is published in the completed source paper ( Undocumented relevance ). Benchmark Relevance Pre-discovery query Author annotation Undocumented relevance Queries | 𝒬 | |\mathcal{Q}| Corpus | 𝒫 | |\mathcal{P}| SciFact ( Wadden et al., 2020 ) Claim support ✗ ✗ ✗ 1.4K 5.2K DORIS-MAE ( Wang et al., 2023 ) Multi-aspect relevance ✗ ✗ ✗ 100 100 ScholarQABench ( Asai et al., 2024 ) Claim support ✗ ✗ ✗ 2,967 45M LitSearch ( Ajith et al., 2024 ) Citation relation ✗ ✓ ✗ 597 64K MIR ( Garikaparthi et al., 2025 ) Methodological citation intent ✓ ✗ ✗ 139 4.7K ScholarCatalyst (ours) Author-judged inspiration ✓ ✓ ✓ 894 191K † LitSearch asks authors to write 246 of its 597 queries to retrieve their own papers. 2 Related Work Scientific discovery using LLMs. Accelerating science is a major opportunity for LLM-based agents, which increasingly can propose relevant hypotheses and research ideas ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Wang et al., 2024b ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . We deliberately ground our task in existing papers . Unlike a newly generated idea, which cannot be verified without running it ( Si et al., 2025 ; Si et al., 2026 ) , a published paper comes with a record of what worked, why, and where it fell short. The same grounding is what lets us collect ground truth, since authors can judge existing papers against what actually advanced their project. Existing scientific-discovery systems likewise draw on prior papers, either starting from a seed or target paper and exploiting its citation graph or metadata ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Liu et al., 2025 ) , while others search a task-specific candidate corpus constructed in advance ( Wang et al., 2024b ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Recent work studies how LLMs can generate scientific insights by combining existing ideas ( He-Yueya et al., 2026 ) , further motivating the need to evaluate which prior work agents choose to draw on. ScholarCatalyst directly addresses this evaluation gap by testing whether scientific agents can retrieve insightful prior ideas for an early-stage research question, guided by project authors’ firsthand experience of what helped their research. Scientific literature retrieval. Existing scientific retrieval benchmarks evaluate how well systems find evidence for claims ( Wadden et al., 2020 ; Wadden et al., 2022 ) , retrieve documents for specified facets ( Mysore et al., 2021 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) , and locate papers given document context or explicit information needs ( Ajith et al., 2024 ; Asai et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2025 ; Park et al., 2025 ; Shao et al., 2025 ) . Whereas existing benchmarks provide a retrieval objective that is explicit in the query, we pose an open-ended problem that requires inferring the latent scientific relevance of papers to an early-stage research idea. MIR ( Garikaparthi et al., 2025 ) comes closest, since its queries also withhold the project’s eventual method, but it derives positives from citation-intent annotations indicating methodological influence ( Lauscher et al., 2022 ) . Rather than inferring relevance from the published record, we elicit directly from paper authors otherwise undocumented data about the research process behind it, including early-stage research questions and relevance judgments. To our knowledge, ScholarCatalyst is the first scientific literature retrieval benchmark grounded in authors’ firsthand accounts of their research process. Information retrieval systems. Lexical retrievers ( Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009 ) and embedding retrievers rank corpus papers through term overlap or learned semantic similarity ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ; Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Shanbhogue et al., 2026 ) . For a given query, these methods rank the corpus once and do not adapt the search to the returned papers. Search agents use LLM reasoning to iteratively formulate queries and invoke these retrievers as tools over multiple turns, enabling more adaptive search for complex information-seeking tasks ( Yao et al., 2022 ; Jin et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . Deep research systems extend this approach with subquestion decomposition, reading, and reflection over longer horizons ( Team et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . However, these agents still access the corpus through a retriever’s top- k k candidates at each step. Recent work instead gives agents direct access to the raw corpus through terminal tools such as grep and file reads, letting the language model determine how to search and interpret documents ( Li et al., 2026 ; Sen et al., 2026 ) . Whether such agentic search approaches can retrieve prior work whose scientific inspiration is latent rather than lexically explicit remains unclear. 3 ScholarCatalyst: Evaluating Scientific Literature Retrieval with Authors’ Firsthand Accounts ScholarCatalyst evaluates whether retrieval systems can identify catalyst papers , prior work whose ideas could inspire and help advance an early stage of research. To obtain firsthand judgments about inspiration, we ask project authors which prior papers did or could have helped advance their project and why, knowledge that is largely absent from the public record. We first define the task of retrieving useful prior work, including its query types, retrieval corpus, and evaluation metrics ( Section 3.1 ). We then describe our pipeline that supports effective and efficient data collection ( Section 3.2 ) and the subsequent author validation and revision process for finalizing the benchmark instances ( Section 3.3 ). Figure 2: An example ScholarCatalyst instance. For each query q q , we also provide hard-negative documents, 𝒟 q − ⊂ 𝒫 < S \smash{\mathcal{D}^{-}_{q}\subset\mathcal{P}_{<S}} , which are related to q q but did not inspire the authors of S S . Each query q q is a short paragraph that reconstructs the research landscape at the outset of the project underlying the source paper S S . It describes what was known, what remained unresolved, and the open question the authors set out to answer, without revealing the eventual solution. The hard-negative set 𝒟 q − ⊆ 𝒫 < S ∖ 𝒟 q + \smash{\mathcal{D}^{-}_{q}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{<S}\setminus\mathcal{D}^{+}_{q}} contains papers that the authors reviewed and rejected. We additionally retrieve uncited candidates with BM25 and Qwen3-Embedding-8B ( Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) . Gemini 3.6 Flash ( Google DeepMind, 2026b ) reranks the pooled candidates for scientific relevance, and the pipeline retains 10 candidates per query to balance coverage of potential false negatives with a manageable author-review workload. The resulting pre-annotations and candidates are loaded into a web interface for author review ( Section 3.3 ). We describe the implementation details of our pipeline in Appendix E . Our automated data-collection pipeline constructs a retrieval corpus and author-review materials, including structured paper data and candidate papers ( Section 3.2 ), which authors review through our interface to validate and revise queries, judge candidate-paper relevance, and provide rationales ( Section 3.3 ). items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.02200 (cs) [Submitted on 1 Oct 2026] Title: VISTA: A Visual Harness for Reasoning in an Interactive World Authors: Qiushi Han , Keya Hu , Linlu Qiu , Cathy Wu , Kaiming He View a PDF of the paper titled VISTA: A Visual Harness for Reasoning in an Interactive World, by Qiushi Han and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: We show that multimodal models possess strong reasoning abilities and that an appropriate harness can unlock their potential to solve tasks across diverse interactive environments. We introduce VISTA, a visual harness that gives a general-purpose multimodal model long-horizon vision. VISTA allows the model to directly perceive the environment through visual observations and maintains a lossless visual memory that preserves past observations in their original form. The model can actively retrieve these observations and reorganize its visual input as it reasons. On ARC-AGI-3, VISTA improves Claude Opus 5.0's Relative Human Action Efficiency score from 40.68 to a perfect 100.00, with the model completing all 25 public games using 57.4% fewer actions than first-time human participants. VISTA's simple design also allows it to extend naturally to diverse visual environments with minimal adaptation. Across three additional benchmarks covering a diverse range of visual games and puzzles, it substantially outperforms baselines using the same underlying model with minimal harnesses. Our results highlight VISTA's potential as a general-purpose visual harness for advancing multimodal agents in complex visual environments. Comments: Tech report. items.content: VISTA: A Visual Harness for Reasoning in an Interactive World Qiushi Han * Keya Hu * Linlu Qiu * Cathy Wu Kaiming He Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Code: https://github.com/joshhhhhan/VISTA Abstract We show that multimodal models possess strong reasoning abilities and that an appropriate harness can unlock their potential to solve tasks across diverse interactive environments. We introduce VISTA , a visual harness that gives a general-purpose multimodal model long-horizon vision. VISTA allows the model to directly perceive the environment through visual observations and maintains a lossless visual memory that preserves past observations in their original form. The model can actively retrieve these observations and reorganize its visual input as it reasons. On ARC-AGI-3, VISTA improves Claude Opus 5.0’s Relative Human Action Efficiency score from 40.68 to a perfect 100.00, with the model completing all 25 public games using 57.4% fewer actions than first-time human participants. VISTA’s simple design also allows it to extend naturally to diverse visual environments with minimal adaptation. Across three additional benchmarks covering a diverse range of visual games and puzzles, it substantially outperforms baselines using the same underlying model with minimal harnesses. Our results highlight VISTA’s potential as a general-purpose visual harness for advancing multimodal agents in complex visual environments. † † footnotetext: * Co-first authors. Email: {joshhan, keya_hu, linluqiu, cathywu, kaiming}@mit.edu 1 Introduction Figure 1: Comparison of different agent designs. (a) Language agents reason over textual observations. (b) Multimodal agents encode images into visual representations only once, but these representations may be compressed, lossy, and insufficient for subsequent reasoning, potentially limiting the models’ reasoning capabilities. (c) VISTA allows the multimodal model to iteratively call visual tools to retrieve past visual observations and reorganize its visual input as it reasons. For simplicity, we show the VLM as a vision transformer (ViT) encoder followed by an LLM. The two VLM blocks represent the same underlying model. We live in a dynamic, high-dimensional world. As humans, we perceive our surroundings, reason about what we observe, and act based on our understanding and past experience [ 56 , 48 ] . However, it remains unclear whether existing artificial intelligence (AI) systems have a similar ability to understand and interact robustly with the world, especially in unfamiliar environments. To study this question, we use ARC-AGI-3 [ 5 ] , a suite of interactive visual games in which an agent needs to discover the rules and goals of unfamiliar worlds through interaction. This benchmark is typically approached as a language-based problem, with large language models (LLMs) receiving a textual or structured representation of the environment, as shown in Figure 1 a. Building on this setup, a common strategy is to use code-based methods that construct a executable world model using symbolic programs [ 62 , 39 , 11 , 25 ] . We instead reframe ARC-AGI-3 as a vision-based problem and address it using multimodal models. However, as illustrated in Figure 1 b, existing vision-language models (VLMs) typically encode each image once into visual representations [ 2 , 28 ] . These representations may not preserve the details needed as reasoning evolves. Moreover, earlier observations may be removed from the context or replaced by textual summaries to stay within the model’s context limit [ 29 , 36 , 27 ] . These limitations may constrain the models’ reasoning capabilities during long-horizon interactions. To this end, we introduce VISTA , a visual harness that allows the model to actively reorganize its visual input during long-horizon interactions (Figure 1 c). The model receives visual observations of the environment that preserve the appearance and spatial relations of objects. It develops its understanding of the environment through free-form language reasoning [ 55 , 42 ] and uses this understanding to predict action outcomes and plan subsequent actions [ 59 ] . Instead of relying solely on visual representations retained in the model’s context, which may be compressed, lossy, and insufficient for subsequent reasoning, VISTA maintains a lossless visual memory . This memory stores every frame returned by the environment, including intermediate animation frames, in its original form. The model can retrieve observations from this memory through visual inspection , selecting frames to compare and spatial regions to examine at different levels of detail based on its current reasoning needs [ 48 , 47 ] . Figure 2 shows two example agent trajectories with VISTA, illustrating how observation, reasoning, inspection, and action are interleaved. With VISTA, Claude Opus 5.0 [ 3 ] completes all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games with a Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE) score of 100.00 with xhigh reasoning effort, using 57.4% fewer actions than the first-time human baseline. VISTA with GPT-5.6 Sol [ 33 ] likewise completes all 25 games, achieving an RHAE score of 99.00 with max reasoning effort. To our knowledge, VISTA is the first vision-based system to achieve perfect or near-perfect performance on ARC-AGI-3 without program synthesis. For comparison, the organizers’ official baselines, which also do not use programs, achieve RHAE scores of 40.68 with Opus 5.0 high and 13.33 with GPT-5.6 Sol max [ 7 , 34 ] . The simplicity of VISTA also allows it to extend naturally to other visual environments with minimal adaptation. We apply the same visual harness to 34 browser games from GameWorld [ 35 ] , 10 browser games from AI GameStore [ 60 ] , and 39 visual tracking problems from BabyVision [ 12 ] . Together, these benchmarks cover a wide range of games and visual reasoning tasks that require skills such as complex reasoning, spatial navigation, and strategic planning. GPT-5.6 Sol with VISTA substantially outperforms baselines that use the same model with minimal harnesses. It also outperforms the novice human baseline on GameWorld and the human median baseline on AI GameStore. Overall, these results demonstrate VISTA’s effectiveness across diverse visual environments and highlight visual harness design as an important direction for improving multimodal agents. Figure 2: VISTA trajectories on ARC-AGI-3 (left) and GameWorld (right). The harness allows the agent to directly observe the visual states, reason in natural language, and inspect its lossless visual memory at the original level of detail when needed. 2 Related Work ARC-AGI benchmarks. ARC-AGI-1 [ 16 ] and ARC-AGI-2 [ 14 ] are benchmarks designed to evaluate abstract reasoning over static input–output grids [ 15 ] . Approaches to these benchmarks often use pretrained large language models [ 8 , 1 , 19 , 37 , 26 , 9 ] , recurrent models [ 50 , 23 ] , or vision-based models [ 22 ] . ARC-AGI-3 [ 5 ] makes this setting interactive: an agent must explore novel environments, adapt continuously from its interactions, and take actions to achieve its goals [ 24 ] . Existing approaches to ARC-AGI-3 largely rely on program synthesis [ 62 , 25 , 11 , 39 , 40 ] , in which agents perceive the environment through textual or symbolic representations and abstract it into programs that can be executed, verified, and searched over to guide actions. While effective on ARC-AGI-3, these approaches rely on constructing explicit programmatic abstractions of the environment. As environments become more visually complex, representing their states, transition dynamics, and goal conditions with explicit programs may become increasingly difficult. In contrast, VISTA operates directly on visual observations and reasons in natural language. Computer-use agents. Recent work has explored agents that interact with computers and graphical user interfaces to complete complex tasks. Existing approaches broadly differ in their observation space. Text-based approaches operate over structured representations of the interface, such as HTML, DOM trees, accessibility trees, or element identifiers, and use language models to reason over these representations and take symbolic actions [ 32 , 17 , 64 ] . Vision-based computer-use agents interact directly with screenshots and take grounded actions such as clicks, mouse movements, and keyboard inputs [ 13 , 57 , 38 , 52 , 30 ] . VISTA follows the vision-based paradigm: the agent reasons directly from visual observations rather than textual or symbolic representations of the environment. It focuses on a visual-centric harness for reasoning in interactive worlds and provides a simple interface for agents to observe and interact with the environment. Game-playing agents. Games have long served as testbeds for developing agents that learn to perceive, reason, and act in interactive environments. Classical approaches learn policies through reinforcement learning [ 31 , 43 , 44 ] or learn environment dynamics to support prediction and planning [ 41 , 21 ] . While these methods provide general learning algorithms, they typically require training a separate agent for each game. More recently, foundation models have enabled more general-purpose agents that operate in richer game environments. Voyager uses a large language model together with structured Minecraft observations and an executable skill library [ 51 ] , while JARVIS-1 incorporates visual observations and retrieves similar past experiences for planning in Minecraft [ 53 ] . Generalist agents such as SIMA and SIMA 2 [ 46 , 45 ] , Cradle [ 49 ] , and Game-TARS [ 54 ] further operate directly from visual observations across multiple environments. A central challenge in these systems is retaining information over long interaction horizons: prior agents typically maintain only a bounded visual context or selectively store and compress past experiences. VISTA instead preserves the complete visual interaction history losslessly and allows the agent to actively revisit arbitrary previous frames and regions during reasoning. 3 VISTA: A Visual Harness Figure 3: VISTA’s key design components and per-turn pipeline. We use ARC-AGI-3 as an example. (a) Visual observations : The model receives rendered visual states. (b) Lossless visual memory : Every returned frame is stored in its original form. (c) Model-directed visual inspection : The model selects frames and regions to examine during reasoning. (d) Per-turn pipeline : The agent observes, reasons, and acts, while each returned frame is preserved in visual memory. Revisiting past observations and updating notes are optional steps directed by the model. VISTA lets the model directly perceive the environment through visual inputs. However, existing multimodal systems typically encode visual observations once and discard the raw inputs. As the context fills, these representations may be removed or replaced by textual summaries, and the model may not control what is retained. More importantly, the model may not know at encoding time which visual information will matter later: a representation sufficient at one stage may omit details required in subsequent reasoning steps. These limitations directly motivate the design of VISTA, which preserves original observations in a lossless visual memory and provides tools for the model to retrieve and inspect them during interaction. This allows the model to revisit visual evidence and reorganize its visual input as it reasons, without requiring all relevant information to be captured in the initial visual encoding and retained in the model’s context. 3.1 Visual Harness Components We introduce three key visual harness components: visual observations , which allows the agent to perceive the environment through rendered images; lossless visual memory , which preserves visual observations in their original form; and visual inspection , which allows the model to revisit visual evidence and examine details as needed. Together, these components provide the model with an explicit attention mechanism over the interaction history, allowing it to select which frames and regions to examine during reasoning. Visual observation. The model receives visual observations from the environment (Figure. 3 a). These observations preserve the appearance and spatial relation of objects, allowing the model to use its learned visual priors to interpret and reason about the environment. Lossless visual memory. The harness stores every frame returned by the environment, including intermediate animation frames, in its original form (Figure. 3 b). Each frame is indexed by turn and frame number and remains available throughout the interaction, independently of what is retained in the model’s current context. Visual inspection. Building on the visual memory, we provide the agent with tools to actively inspect visual information in space and across time (Figure 3 c). In space , it can request an enlarged view of any rectangular region from the original frame, allowing it to examine fine-grained details that may be difficult to perceive in the full image. Across time , it can retrieve and inspect multiple frames from arbitrary earlier turns to revisit past visual evidence, compare states, and replay how an action unfolded through its intermediate animation frames. At each turn, the model is free to decide whether to inspect its visual memory and which frames or regions to examine. 3.2 Pipeline In our pipeline, the model and the harness interact through a multi-turn conversation (Figure 2 ). The harness is purely mechanical and does not involve any trained model: it executes tool calls requested by the model, returns outputs such as images or pixel values, and reports errors for invalid requests. The model reasons over these outputs and issues its next request to the harness if needed. A single agent interacts with each game throughout the run. Each game turn may include multiple exchanges with the harness before the agent executes one game action (Figure 3 d). At the start of a turn, the agent receives the current visual state and available actions. It can also consult two notes that it maintains: GUIDE.md , which records its understanding of the game and information that may remain useful across levels, and WORKING.md , which serves as a scratchpad for the current state. Through inspect , the agent can revisit earlier observations, including intermediate animation frames produced by its previous actions. It can also use read_pixels to examine pixel values within a selected region. Consulting the notes and using the inspection tools are optional and left to the agent’s decision. The agent uses free-form language to reason and plan. It predicts the outcome of its planned action, revises its notes to reflect its updated understanding of the environment, and calls play to execute the chosen action and advance to the next game turn. When its context approaches the limit, the agent writes a concise handoff summary and resumes from the current state in a fresh context. Its notes ( GUIDE.md and WORKING.md ), visual memory, and action history remain available. Every game uses the same interface and short prompt as shown in Appendix A.5 . The available tools (e.g., inspect , read_pixels , and play ), together with their pseudocode and corresponding descriptions are provided to the agent, as shown in Appendix A.4 ). 4 VISTA on ARC-AGI-3 4.1 Setup Dataset. ARC-AGI-3 [ 5 ] consists of interactive visual games whose rules and objectives are not provided explicitly. We evaluate on the 25 public games. At each step, the agent observes the current visual state, selects an available action, and uses the resulting observation to infer object roles, transition rules, hidden states, and possible goals. Each game contains multiple levels that share underlying mechanics while introducing new concepts, objects, layouts, or constraints. The agent therefore needs to retain and apply previously inferred knowledge across levels while continually adapting its understanding through interaction. Figure 4 shows an example agent trajectory. Evaluation metrics. Performance is measured by Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE) [ 4 ] , which compares an agent’s action efficiency with that of first-time human players. A completed level receives 100% credit when its action count matches the human baseline, up to 115% when it uses fewer actions, and partial credit when it uses more actions. Unfinished levels receive zero credit. Later levels receive greater weight, and each game score is capped by the weighted fraction of levels completed. See Appendix A.3 for details. Models. We instantiate VISTA with two general-purpose, closed-weight multimodal model backends commonly used in prior work. Each backend is evaluated independently under the same interaction protocol. We use Claude Opus 5.0 [ 3 ] run with extra-high reasoning effort through the Claude Code CLI and GPT-5.6 Sol [ 33 ] run with max reasoning effort through the Codex CLI. 4.2 Results Table 1: System-level comparison on 25 public games of ARC-AGI-3. VISTA is, to our knowledge, the first system to achieve perfect or near-perfect performance without program synthesis. System Program Model Effort RHAE Official impl. [ 5 ] No GPT-5.6 Sol [ 34 ] max 13.33 Opus 5.0 † high 40.68 Schema [ 62 ] Yes GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh → \rightarrow max 95.35 Opus 4.8 → \rightarrow Fable 5 max 98.98 ewma_sv_v1.6 [ 39 ] Yes GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh 98.97 Retrodict [ 11 ] Yes GPT-5.6 Sol max 99.86 Tycho [ 25 ] Yes GPT-5.6 Sol max 100.00 Opus 5.0 xhigh 100.00 VISTA No GPT-5.6 Sol max 99.00 Opus 5.0 xhigh 100.00 † Calculated from the officially reported per-game scores for the 25 public games [ 6 ] . Table 1 shows a system-level comparison on the 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, unless otherwise noted. With Claude Opus 5.0, VISTA achieves a perfect RHAE score of 100.00, matching other state-of-the-art systems. It uses 7,302 actions in total, 57.4% fewer than the human reference of 17,135 actions. Figure 4: Example trajectory in ARC-AGI-3. Each frame is labeled with its turn and action; × N \times N denotes repeated actions. Boxes mark targets, and rings mark the agent’s clicks. The agent must infer the rules: black pieces move together with their reflections across the mirror line, and all yellow targets must be covered. Level 3 introduces a movable horizontal mirror line and selectable pieces. Most of the compared systems come from concurrent work. These systems typically represent observations as text-based numerical grids and often reason using a code-based world model: the agent abstracts the environment into symbolic programs that can be executed and checked during exploration. To our knowledge, VISTA is the first system to achieve perfect or near-perfect performance on ARC-AGI-3 without program synthesis . For comparison, the same model scores only 40.68 under the official implementation. In Figure 6 , we also compare textual grids with our default image observations. We find that visual observations achieve comparable performance with fewer actions while using significantly fewer tokens. 4.3 Ablations For all ablations, we use GPT-5.6 Sol with max reasoning effort and a 200K-token context limit as the default setting. The agent receives a 512 × 512 512\times 512 PNG image of the current rendered state, obtained by 8 × 8\times nearest-neighbor upscaling of the official 64 × 64 64\times 64 frame. Figure 5: Harness configurations on ARC-AGI-3. GPT-5.6 Sol under progressively richer harness configurations, evaluated using (a) RHAE, (b) the total number of actions taken across the 25 games, and (c) the percentage of the 25 games completed. For reference, the official implementation using textual grids (hatched gray bars) achieves a reported RHAE score of 13.33 with 10,619 actions [ 7 , 34 ] . (i) The official implementation with PNG images replacing its textual grid observations. (ii) Increases the action and time limits to match our evaluation protocol (up to 2,000 actions per game) instead of the official stopping criteria. (iii) Adds a continuous conversation, using the model’s native compaction to continue past its context limit. (iv) Adds the two notes, GUIDE.md and WORKING.md , and encourages the agent to build a compact and revisable model of the game. (v) Adds lossless visual memory and inspection. (vi) Adds exact pixel readout, completing VISTA. Configurations (i)–(iv) automatically receive up to seven frames per action, following the official protocol; configurations (v)–(vi) introduce VISTA’s key visual components: the agent automatically receives only the final frame and can actively inspect its visual memory as it reasons. See Appendix A.2 for details. Effects of VISTA components. We compare GPT-5.6 Sol under progressively richer harness configurations in Figure 5 . The official implementation uses textual grids and has a reported RHAE score of 13.33 with 10,619 actions [ 7 , 34 ] . Replacing these textual grids with rendered PNG images (i) increases the score to 47.32, demonstrating the importance of visual observations. The low action count is partly due to runs reaching the action or time limit before completing the games, as suggested by the low completion rate in this configuration. Increasing the action and time limits improves the score to 51.66 (ii). In (iii), we introduce a minimal agent harness that maintains a continuous conversation and uses native compaction to continue beyond its context limit, improving the score to 65.82. Configuration (iv) adds two note files, GUIDE.md and WORKING.md , along with instructions encouraging the agent to build a compact and revisable model of the game, further improving the score to 70.05 (see the prompt in Appendix A.5 ). Finally, configurations (v)–(vi) introduce VISTA’s key visual harness components: adding lossless visual memory and model-directed inspection (v) improves the score to 94.10, while exact pixel readout (vi), which provides numerical RGB values for selected pixels, completes the VISTA harness and increases the score to 99.00. Figure 6: Comparison of observation representations on ARC-AGI-3. (a) An example game state shown as a flattened text grid and a 2D image; the displayed text grid is cropped from the full 64 × 64 64\times 64 grid. (b) RHAE, total actions across the 25 games, and average token usage per game for the two observation representations. Reasoning directly from images. Prior approaches to ARC-AGI-3 commonly represent each frame as a textual grid, encoding observations as rows of integer color indices [ 62 , 39 , 11 , 25 ] . In contrast, VISTA reasons directly from rendered images. We ablate this design choice by replacing VISTA’s image observations with textual grids while keeping the rest of the harness unchanged. As shown in Figure 6 , using textual grids maintains comparable performance but slightly increases the total number of actions. Textual grids are also substantially more token-intensive: a 64 × 64 64\times 64 grid requires roughly 4,000 tokens, compared with approximately 308 image tokens for our default 512 × 512 512\times 512 observation. Token usage per game is 71.9M with textual grids and 30.7M with image observations. Figure 7: Ablations on ARC-AGI-3. Left column : RHAE. Middle column : the total number of actions taken across the 25 games. Right column : the average number of tokens per game. (a): maximum context size, which sets when context compaction occurs. (b): input image scale relative to the official 64 × 64 64\times 64 frame; scales of 2 × 2\times , 4 × 4\times , 8 × 8\times , and 16 × 16\times correspond to 128, 256, 512, and 1,024 pixels per side and roughly 20, 77, 308, and 1,229 image tokens per frame, respectively. Effect of maximum context size. We vary VISTA’s maximum context size, which determines how much interaction history is retained before the agent

On ARC-AGI-3, VISTA improves Claude Opus 5.0’s Relative Human Action Efficiency score from 40.68 to a perfect 100.00, with the model completing all 25 public games using 57.4% fewer actions than first-time human participants. VISTA’s simple design also allows it to extend naturally to diverse visual environments with minimal adaptation. Across three additional benchmarks covering a diverse range of visual games and puzzles, it substantially outperforms baselines using the same underlying model with minimal harnesses. Our results highlight VISTA’s potential as a general-purpose visual harness for advancing multimodal agents in complex visual environments. † † footnotetext: * Co-first authors. Email: {joshhan, keya_hu, linluqiu, cathywu, kaiming}@mit.edu 1 Introduction Figure 1: Comparison of different agent designs. (a) Language agents reason over textual observations. (b) Multimodal agents encode images into visual representations only once, but these representations may be compressed, lossy, and insufficient for subsequent reasoning, potentially limiting the models’ reasoning capabilities. (c) VISTA allows the multimodal model to iteratively call visual tools to retrieve past visual observations and reorganize its visual input as it reasons. For simplicity, we show the VLM as a vision transformer (ViT) encoder followed by an LLM. The two VLM blocks represent the same underlying model. We live in a dynamic, high-dimensional world. As humans, we perceive our surroundings, reason about what we observe, and act based on our understanding and past experience [ 56 , 48 ] . However, it remains unclear whether existing artificial intelligence (AI) systems have a similar ability to understand and interact robustly with the world, especially in unfamiliar environments. To study this question, we use ARC-AGI-3 [ 5 ] , a suite of interactive visual games in which an agent needs to discover the rules and goals of unfamiliar worlds through interaction. This benchmark is typically approached as a language-based problem, with large language models (LLMs) receiving a textual or structured representation of the environment, as shown in Figure 1 a. Building on this setup, a common strategy is to use code-based methods that construct a executable world model using symbolic programs [ 62 , 39 , 11 , 25 ] . We instead reframe ARC-AGI-3 as a vision-based problem and address it using multimodal models. However, as illustrated in Figure 1 b, existing vision-language models (VLMs) typically encode each image once into visual representations [ 2 , 28 ] . These representations may not preserve the details needed as reasoning evolves. Moreover, earlier observations may be removed from the context or replaced by textual summaries to stay within the model’s context limit [ 29 , 36 , 27 ] . These limitations may constrain the models’ reasoning capabilities during long-horizon interactions. To this end, we introduce VISTA , a visual harness that allows the model to actively reorganize its visual input during long-horizon interactions (Figure 1 c). The model receives visual observations of the environment that preserve the appearance and spatial relations of objects. It develops its understanding of the environment through free-form language reasoning [ 55 , 42 ] and uses this understanding to predict action outcomes and plan subsequent actions [ 59 ] . Instead of relying solely on visual representations retained in the model’s context, which may be compressed, lossy, and insufficient for subsequent reasoning, VISTA maintains a lossless visual memory . This memory stores every frame returned by the environment, including intermediate animation frames, in its original form. The model can retrieve observations from this memory through visual inspection , selecting frames to compare and spatial regions to examine at different levels of detail based on its current reasoning needs [ 48 , 47 ] . Figure 2 shows two example agent trajectories with VISTA, illustrating how observation, reasoning, inspection, and action are interleaved. With VISTA, Claude Opus 5.0 [ 3 ] completes all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games with a Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE) score of 100.00 with xhigh reasoning effort, using 57.4% fewer actions than the first-time human baseline. VISTA with GPT-5.6 Sol [ 33 ] likewise completes all 25 games, achieving an RHAE score of 99.00 with max reasoning effort. To our knowledge, VISTA is the first vision-based system to achieve perfect or near-perfect performance on ARC-AGI-3 without program synthesis. For comparison, the organizers’ official baselines, which also do not use programs, achieve RHAE scores of 40.68 with Opus 5.0 high and 13.33 with GPT-5.6 Sol max [ 7 , 34 ] . The simplicity of VISTA also allows it to extend naturally to other visual environments with minimal adaptation. We apply the same visual harness to 34 browser games from GameWorld [ 35 ] , 10 browser games from AI GameStore [ 60 ] , and 39 visual tracking problems from BabyVision [ 12 ] . Together, these benchmarks cover a wide range of games and visual reasoning tasks that require skills such as complex reasoning, spatial navigation, and strategic planning. GPT-5.6 Sol with VISTA substantially outperforms baselines that use the same model with minimal harnesses. It also outperforms the novice human baseline on GameWorld and the human median baseline on AI GameStore. Overall, these results demonstrate VISTA’s effectiveness across diverse visual environments and highlight visual harness design as an important direction for improving multimodal agents. Figure 2: VISTA trajectories on ARC-AGI-3 (left) and GameWorld (right). The harness allows the agent to directly observe the visual states, reason in natural language, and inspect its lossless visual memory at the original level of detail when needed. 2 Related Work ARC-AGI benchmarks. ARC-AGI-1 [ 16 ] and ARC-AGI-2 [ 14 ] are benchmarks designed to evaluate abstract reasoning over static input–output grids [ 15 ] . Approaches to these benchmarks often use pretrained large language models [ 8 , 1 , 19 , 37 , 26 , 9 ] , recurrent models [ 50 , 23 ] , or vision-based models [ 22 ] . ARC-AGI-3 [ 5 ] makes this setting interactive: an agent must explore novel environments, adapt continuously from its interactions, and take actions to achieve its goals [ 24 ] . Existing approaches to ARC-AGI-3 largely rely on program synthesis [ 62 , 25 , 11 , 39 , 40 ] , in which agents perceive the environment through textual or symbolic representations and abstract it into programs that can be executed, verified, and searched over to guide actions. While effective on ARC-AGI-3, these approaches rely on constructing explicit programmatic abstractions of the environment. As environments become more visually complex, representing their states, transition dynamics, and goal conditions with explicit programs may become increasingly difficult. In contrast, VISTA operates directly on visual observations and reasons in natural language. Computer-use agents. Recent work has explored agents that interact with computers and graphical user interfaces to complete complex tasks. Existing approaches broadly differ in their observation space. Text-based approaches operate over structured representations of the interface, such as HTML, DOM trees, accessibility trees, or element identifiers, and use language models to reason over these representations and take symbolic actions [ 32 , 17 , 64 ] . Vision-based computer-use agents interact directly with screenshots and take grounded actions such as clicks, mouse movements, and keyboard inputs [ 13 , 57 , 38 , 52 , 30 ] . VISTA follows the vision-based paradigm: the agent reasons directly from visual observations rather than textual or symbolic representations of the environment. It focuses on a visual-centric harness for reasoning in interactive worlds and provides a simple interface for agents to observe and interact with the environment. Game-playing agents. Games have long served as testbeds for developing agents that learn to perceive, reason, and act in interactive environments. Classical approaches learn policies through reinforcement learning [ 31 , 43 , 44 ] or learn environment dynamics to support prediction and planning [ 41 , 21 ] . While these methods provide general learning algorithms, they typically require training a separate agent for each game. More recently, foundation models have enabled more general-purpose agents that operate in richer game environments. Voyager uses a large language model together with structured Minecraft observations and an executable skill library [ 51 ] , while JARVIS-1 incorporates visual observations and retrieves similar past experiences for planning in Minecraft [ 53 ] . Generalist agents such as SIMA and SIMA 2 [ 46 , 45 ] , Cradle [ 49 ] , and Game-TARS [ 54 ] further operate directly from visual observations across multiple environments. A central challenge in these systems is retaining information over long interaction horizons: prior agents typically maintain only a bounded visual context or selectively store and compress past experiences. VISTA instead preserves the complete visual interaction history losslessly and allows the agent to actively revisit arbitrary previous frames and regions during reasoning. 3 VISTA: A Visual Harness Figure 3: VISTA’s key design components and per-turn pipeline. We use ARC-AGI-3 as an example. (a) Visual observations : The model receives rendered visual states. (b) Lossless visual memory : Every returned frame is stored in its original form. (c) Model-directed visual inspection : The model selects frames and regions to examine during reasoning. (d) Per-turn pipeline : The agent observes, reasons, and acts, while each returned frame is preserved in visual memory. Revisiting past observations and updating notes are optional steps directed by the model. VISTA lets the model directly perceive the environment through visual inputs. However, existing multimodal systems typically encode visual observations once and discard the raw inputs. As the context fills, these representations may be removed or replaced by textual summaries, and the model may not control what is retained. More importantly, the model may not know at encoding time which visual information will matter later: a representation sufficient at one stage may omit details required in subsequent reasoning steps. These limitations directly motivate the design of VISTA, which preserves original observations in a lossless visual memory and provides tools for the model to retrieve and inspect them during interaction. This allows the model to revisit visual evidence and reorganize its visual input as it reasons, without requiring all relevant information to be captured in the initial visual encoding and retained in the model’s context. 3.1 Visual Harness Components We introduce three key visual harness components: visual observations , which allows the agent to perceive the environment through rendered images; lossless visual memory , which preserves visual observations in their original form; and visual inspection , which allows the model to revisit visual evidence and examine details as needed. Together, these components provide the model with an explicit attention mechanism over the interaction history, allowing it to select which frames and regions to examine during reasoning. Visual observation. The model receives visual observations from the environment (Figure. 3 a). These observations preserve the appearance and spatial relation of objects, allowing the model to use its learned visual priors to interpret and reason about the environment. Lossless visual memory. The harness stores every frame returned by the environment, including intermediate animation frames, in its original form (Figure. 3 b). Each frame is indexed by turn and frame number and remains available throughout the interaction, independently of what is retained in the model’s current context. Visual inspection. Building on the visual memory, we provide the agent with tools to actively inspect visual information in space and across time (Figure 3 c). In space , it can request an enlarged view of any rectangular region from the original frame, allowing it to examine fine-grained details that may be difficult to perceive in the full image. Across time , it can retrieve and inspect multiple frames from arbitrary earlier turns to revisit past visual evidence, compare states, and replay how an action unfolded through its intermediate animation frames. At each turn, the model is free to decide whether to inspect its visual memory and which frames or regions to examine. 3.2 Pipeline In our pipeline, the model and the harness interact through a multi-turn conversation (Figure 2 ). The harness is purely mechanical and does not involve any trained model: it executes tool calls requested by the model, returns outputs such as images or pixel values, and reports errors for invalid requests. The model reasons over these outputs and issues its next request to the harness if needed. A single agent interacts with each game throughout the run. Each game turn may include multiple exchanges with the harness before the agent executes one game action (Figure 3 d). At the start of a turn, the agent receives the current visual state and available actions. It can also consult two notes that it maintains: GUIDE.md , which records its understanding of the game and information that may remain useful across levels, and WORKING.md , which serves as a scratchpad for the current state. Through inspect , the agent can revisit earlier observations, including intermediate animation frames produced by its previous actions. It can also use read_pixels to examine pixel values within a selected region. Consulting the notes and using the inspection tools are optional and left to the agent’s decision. The agent uses free-form language to reason and plan. It predicts the outcome of its planned action, revises its notes to reflect its updated understanding of the environment, and calls play to execute the chosen action and advance to the next game turn. When its context approaches the limit, the agent writes a concise handoff summary and resumes from the current state in a fresh context. Its notes ( GUIDE.md and WORKING.md ), visual memory, and action history remain available. Every game uses the same interface and short prompt as shown in Appendix A.5 . The available tools (e.g., inspect , read_pixels , and play ), together with their pseudocode and corresponding descriptions are provided to the agent, as shown in Appendix A.4 ). 4 VISTA on ARC-AGI-3 4.1 Setup Dataset. ARC-AGI-3 [ 5 ] consists of interactive visual games whose rules and objectives are not provided explicitly. We evaluate on the 25 public games. At each step, the agent observes the current visual state, selects an available action, and uses the resulting observation to infer object roles, transition rules, hidden states, and possible goals. Each game contains multiple levels that share underlying mechanics while introducing new concepts, objects, layouts, or constraints. The agent therefore needs to retain and apply previously inferred knowledge across levels while continually adapting its understanding through interaction. Figure 4 shows an example agent trajectory. Evaluation metrics. Performance is measured by Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE) [ 4 ] , which compares an agent’s action efficiency with that of first-time human players. A completed level receives 100% credit when its action count matches the human baseline, up to 115% when it uses fewer actions, and partial credit when it uses more actions. Unfinished levels receive zero credit. Later levels receive greater weight, and each game score is capped by the weighted fraction of levels completed. See Appendix A.3 for details. Models. We instantiate VISTA with two general-purpose, closed-weight multimodal model backends commonly used in prior work. Each backend is evaluated independently under the same interaction protocol. We use Claude Opus 5.0 [ 3 ] run with extra-high reasoning effort through the Claude Code CLI and GPT-5.6 Sol [ 33 ] run with max reasoning effort through the Codex CLI. 4.2 Results Table 1: System-level comparison on 25 public games of ARC-AGI-3. VISTA is, to our knowledge, the first system to achieve perfect or near-perfect performance without program synthesis. System Program Model Effort RHAE Official impl. [ 5 ] No GPT-5.6 Sol [ 34 ] max 13.33 Opus 5.0 † high 40.68 Schema [ 62 ] Yes GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh → \rightarrow max 95.35 Opus 4.8 → \rightarrow Fable 5 max 98.98 ewma_sv_v1.6 [ 39 ] Yes GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh 98.97 Retrodict [ 11 ] Yes GPT-5.6 Sol max 99.86 Tycho [ 25 ] Yes GPT-5.6 Sol max 100.00 Opus 5.0 xhigh 100.00 VISTA No GPT-5.6 Sol max 99.00 Opus 5.0 xhigh 100.00 † Calculated from the officially reported per-game scores for the 25 public games [ 6 ] . Table 1 shows a system-level comparison on the 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, unless otherwise noted. With Claude Opus 5.0, VISTA achieves a perfect RHAE score of 100.00, matching other state-of-the-art systems. It uses 7,302 actions in total, 57.4% fewer than the human reference of 17,135 actions. Figure 4: Example trajectory in ARC-AGI-3. Each frame is labeled with its turn and action; × N \times N denotes repeated actions. Boxes mark targets, and rings mark the agent’s clicks. The agent must infer the rules: black pieces move together with their reflections across the mirror line, and all yellow targets must be covered. Level 3 introduces a movable horizontal mirror line and selectable pieces. Most of the compared systems come from concurrent work. These systems typically represent observations as text-based numerical grids and often reason using a code-based world model: the agent abstracts the environment into symbolic programs that can be executed and checked during exploration. To our knowledge, VISTA is the first system to achieve perfect or near-perfect performance on ARC-AGI-3 without program synthesis . For comparison, the same model scores only 40.68 under the official implementation. In Figure 6 , we also compare textual grids with our default image observations. We find that visual observations achieve comparable performance with fewer actions while using significantly fewer tokens. 4.3 Ablations For all ablations, we use GPT-5.6 Sol with max reasoning effort and a 200K-token context limit as the default setting. The agent receives a 512 × 512 512\times 512 PNG image of the current rendered state, obtained by 8 × 8\times nearest-neighbor upscaling of the official 64 × 64 64\times 64 frame. Figure 5: Harness configurations on ARC-AGI-3. GPT-5.6 Sol under progressively richer harness configurations, evaluated using (a) RHAE, (b) the total number of actions taken across the 25 games, and (c) the percentage of the 25 games completed. For reference, the official implementation using textual grids (hatched gray bars) achieves a reported RHAE score of 13.33 with 10,619 actions [ 7 , 34 ] . (i) The official implementation with PNG images replacing its textual grid observations. (ii) Increases the action and time limits to match our evaluation protocol (up to 2,000 actions per game) instead of the official stopping criteria. (iii) Adds a continuous conversation, using the model’s native compaction to continue past its context limit. (iv) Adds the two notes, GUIDE.md and WORKING.md , and encourages the agent to build a compact and revisable model of the game. (v) Adds lossless visual memory and inspection. (vi) Adds exact pixel readout, completing VISTA. Configurations (i)–(iv) automatically receive up to seven frames per action, following the official protocol; configurations (v)–(vi) introduce VISTA’s key visual components: the agent automatically receives only the final frame and can actively inspect its visual memory as it reasons. See Appendix A.2 for details. Effects of VISTA components. We compare GPT-5.6 Sol under progressively richer harness configurations in Figure 5 . The official implementation uses textual grids and has a reported RHAE score of 13.33 with 10,619 actions [ 7 , 34 ] . Replacing these textual grids with rendered PNG images (i) increases the score to 47.32, demonstrating the importance of visual observations. The low action count is partly due to runs reaching the action or time limit before completing the games, as suggested by the low completion rate in this configuration. Increasing the action and time limits improves the score to 51.66 (ii). In (iii), we introduce a minimal agent harness that maintains a continuous conversation and uses native compaction to continue beyond its context limit, improving the score to 65.82. Configuration (iv) adds two note files, GUIDE.md and WORKING.md , along with instructions encouraging the agent to build a compact and revisable model of the game, further improving the score to 70.05 (see the prompt in Appendix A.5 ). Figure 6: Comparison of observation representations on ARC-AGI-3. (a) An example game state shown as a flattened text grid and a 2D image; the displayed text grid is cropped from the full 64 × 64 64\times 64 grid. (b) RHAE, total actions across the 25 games, and average token usage per game for the two observation representations. Reasoning directly from images. Prior approaches to ARC-AGI-3 commonly represent each frame as a textual grid, encoding observations as rows of integer color indices [ 62 , 39 , 11 , 25 ] . In contrast, VISTA reasons directly from rendered images. We ablate this design choice by replacing VISTA’s image observations with textual grids while keeping the rest of the harness unchanged. As shown in Figure 6 , using textual grids maintains comparable performance but slightly increases the total number of actions. Textual grids are also substantially more token-intensive: a 64 × 64 64\times 64 grid requires roughly 4,000 tokens, compared with approximately 308 image tokens for our default 512 × 512 512\times 512 observation. Token usage per game is 71.9M with textual grids and 30.7M with image observations. Figure 7: Ablations on ARC-AGI-3. Left column : RHAE.
